fields.title: The Key Teachings of John Calvin
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of John Calvin’s teaching — the knowledge of God and of ourselves, Scripture as spectacles for dim eyes, union with Christ and its double grace, and the Christian life of self-denial and prayer. Twenty-one short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Calvin’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by John Calvin. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of his teaching into twenty-one short chapters for the ordinary reader, with a chapter on his life, a conclusion and a guide to his books. It draws throughout on his Institutes of the Christian Religion and his commentaries, and on the four of his sermons that sit in the Ochorus library.

Calvin’s one theme was the knowledge of God — not the cold knowledge of a textbook, but the knowledge that makes a person bow, trust and give thanks. We cannot know ourselves truly until we have looked upon God, and we cannot know God as He wishes to be known except in Christ, clothed with His gospel. This volume follows that thread from the opening page of the Institutes through Scripture, providence, sin and grace, union with Christ, faith, self-denial, prayer and election, to the church, the sacraments, the state and the Genevan pulpit. It is honest about the burning of Michael Servetus, the severity of Genevan discipline, the hardness of his teaching on reprobation and the heat of his polemic.

Calvin’s own writings are in the public domain, and older English translations of the Institutes, the commentaries and many sermons are freely available; every chapter here names them so the reader can go to the source. This companion is offered only to open the door. It quotes Scripture from the Authorised (King James) Version, and makes no claim to stand in for the man’s own clear, searching and deeply reverent pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent. JOHN 17:3

Few names in Christian history call up such strong feelings as John Calvin’s, and few are so little read. To some he is the theologian of grace, the teacher who gave the Reformation its mind and taught half of Protestant Europe to read the Bible. To others he is a byword for gloom and severity, the stern magistrate of Geneva who burned a heretic and taught that God had damned most of the human race before it was born. Both pictures are drawn from real things. Neither is the man. The best way to meet Calvin is not through his admirers or his enemies, but through his own pages, and most people who do so are surprised by what they find: a warm, reverent, careful teacher of Scripture, overwhelmed by the goodness of God.

He was a Frenchman, born in 1509 in the cathedral town of Noyon in Picardy, trained in the law, converted in his early twenties, and driven out of France by persecution. He wrote the first edition of his Institutes of the Christian Religion at twenty-six. He meant to live quietly as a scholar and was instead pressed into service at Geneva, a small, quarrelsome city on the edge of the Swiss lands, where, apart from three years of exile in Strasbourg, he spent the rest of his life. He preached there several times a week for over twenty years, wrote commentaries on most of the Bible, trained pastors for France and beyond, and died in 1564, not yet fifty-five, worn out. He asked to be buried without a stone.

Why he still matters

Calvin matters, first, because of his influence, which is hard to overstate. The Reformed churches of France, the Netherlands, Scotland, Hungary and the English Puritans all looked to Geneva. The Presbyterian and Reformed traditions, much of the Baptist and Congregational world, and a great deal of evangelical theology besides, still speak in his accents, often without knowing it.

But he matters more because of what he saw. Calvin was not an innovator; he wanted nothing more than to set out plainly what the Scriptures teach and what the church of the early centuries had believed. What he did have was an extraordinary gift for clarity, order and proportion. In the Institutes he took the great truths of the gospel and set each in its place, so that the reader can see how they belong together — creation and redemption, grace and holiness, faith and prayer, the church and the Christian in the world.

The one thread

If you look for the single thread running through all that Calvin wrote, you find it in the very first sentence of the Institutes. Nearly all the wisdom we possess, he says there, consists of two parts: the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. Everything else in his teaching is those two kinds of knowledge unfolded side by side.

The knowledge Calvin means is never merely in the head. It is knowledge that moves the heart to reverence and trust. He calls it piety: a reverence for God joined with love, which comes from knowing the benefits He gives. To know God is to know Him as Creator and Lord, as the fountain of every good, and above all as a Father who has reconciled us to Himself in Christ. To know ourselves is to know our dignity as His creatures, our ruin as sinners, and our utter dependence on His grace. The two are always held together. We cannot look at God without being humbled, and we cannot see our need without being driven to look at God.

Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me. JEREMIAH 9:23–24

This is why Calvin’s motto, stamped on his seal, showed a hand holding out a heart. It is a picture of what knowing God does. A person who has truly seen God’s goodness gives himself back to Him.

How this book is arranged

The second chapter tells his life. The twenty-one chapters that follow each take one of his key teachings, and they follow the order of the Institutes itself, from the knowledge of God the Creator, through Christ the Redeemer and the way we receive His grace, to the church, the sacraments, civil government and the practical shape of Calvin’s Geneva.

Ochorus hosts four of his sermons, and where Calvin is quoted in these pages it is from those, in their older English translation. The Institutes and the commentaries are described and paraphrased, with the book and chapter of the Institutes named wherever it helps the reader to find the place. Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Calvin would approve. He closed his lectures with prayer, and he taught that prayer is the chief exercise of faith.

Reading him with care

This book is not a monument. Calvin himself asked not to have one. He must be read gratefully, but also honestly, and four matters in particular need to be named.

The first is the death of Michael Servetus. In 1553 the Spanish physician and anti-Trinitarian writer was arrested in Geneva, tried and burned alive. Calvin drew up the charges, sought his conviction and afterwards defended the punishment of heretics in print. Most churches of the time would have done the same; that does not make it right. It stands against the gospel he preached, and it will be faced squarely in these pages.

The second is the discipline of Geneva. The consistory of pastors and elders summoned men and women for drunkenness, quarrelling, dancing, superstition and absence from sermons. Calvin believed discipline was the sinews of the church, and much of it was pastoral. But it could be intrusive and harsh, and it was backed by the power of the city.

The third is his teaching on predestination. Calvin taught not only that God chooses some to salvation by free grace, but that He passes by others and ordains them to just condemnation. He himself called it a dreadful decree. Many who love his teaching on grace cannot follow him all the way here, and the chapter on election will set out both what he said and the pastoral cautions he himself placed around it.

The fourth is his polemic. Calvin wrote against Rome, against the Anabaptists, against Lutheran opponents on the Lord’s Supper and against many others, and he could be scornful and sharp. His sermons in the Ochorus library show it. The reader should learn from his zeal for truth without copying his contempt.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

He was a reserved, ill, anxious and hard-working man who believed God had laid hold of him against his will, and he spent himself for others to the end. He would not want to be admired. He would want you to know God, and to know yourself in His light.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before reading further, write down what you have heard about Calvin and where you heard it. Hold it loosely until you have read him for yourself.

2. Ask yourself honestly which you think about more: God, or yourself. Then ask whether each kind of knowledge is leading you towards the other.

3. Read the first chapter of the Institutes this week; it is only a few pages long.

4. Where a teacher you admire has done wrong, practise naming it plainly without throwing away what was true in him.

5. Set a time each week to read one chapter of this book, and do not move on until you have prayed its prayer.

A PRAYER
Lord God, the only true God, this is life eternal, to know You and Jesus Christ whom You have sent.
Show me Yourself, that I may see myself truly; and show me my need, that I may run to You.
Thank You for Your servant John Calvin, for his clear mind and his reverent heart. Where he was faithful to Your Word, teach me through him; where he sinned and erred, keep me from following.
Take my heart, which I offer to You now, promptly and sincerely, and make it wholly Yours. Amen.

fields.title: The Heart in the Open Hand
fields.body_html:
I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart. PSALM 119:32

A boy of Noyon. John Calvin — Jean Cauvin in his own French — was born on 10 July 1509 at Noyon, a cathedral town in Picardy, in the north of France. His father, Gérard Cauvin, had risen from modest beginnings to become a notary and a man of business for the bishop and cathedral chapter. His mother, Jeanne, died when he was a small child. Gérard was ambitious for his clever son and meant him for the church; the boy was given small church benefices while still young, whose income paid for his schooling. At about fourteen he was sent to Paris, where he studied Latin at the Collège de la Marche under Mathurin Cordier, a gifted and gentle teacher whom he loved all his life, and then at the stricter Collège de Montaigu.

From theology to law. Then his father changed his mind. Gérard had quarrelled with the cathedral chapter at Noyon, and he decided that the law would make his son a better living than the church. So Calvin went to Orléans and then to Bourges to study under some of the leading jurists of France. After his father’s death in 1531 he was free to follow his own tastes, and in 1532 he published his first book, a learned commentary on the Roman philosopher Seneca’s treatise On Clemency. It was the work of a promising young scholar with no obvious interest in reforming the church.

A sudden conversion. Somewhere in these years everything changed. Calvin almost never spoke of himself, but in the preface to his commentary on the Psalms, written a quarter of a century later, he tells us that God, by a sudden conversion, subdued his mind and made it teachable, though it had been more stubborn in such matters than was usual at his age. He names no place and no date. He only names the One who did it. By 1533 he was known among those in Paris who were drawn to the evangelical teaching coming out of Germany and Switzerland, and when his friend Nicolas Cop, the rector of the university, gave an address that autumn that sounded dangerously Lutheran, Calvin was suspected of having helped to write it. He left Paris in haste. In 1534 he returned to Noyon and gave up his church benefices. That October, placards attacking the Mass were posted in Paris and elsewhere, one even reportedly on the king’s own door, and a fierce persecution followed. Calvin left France.

The Institutes. At Basel, under an assumed name, he wrote a book. The first edition of the Institutes of the Christian Religion appeared in March 1536. It was a small book, arranged like a catechism around the Law, the Creed, the Lord’s Prayer and the sacraments, and it opened with a letter to King Francis I, defending the persecuted French evangelicals against the charge that they were rebels and heretics. Calvin was twenty-six. The book made his name. He would spend the rest of his life revising it, and it grew with him, until in its final Latin edition of 1559 it had become four books and eighty chapters.

Seized for Geneva. In the summer of 1536, travelling towards Strasbourg, he was forced by war to take a detour through Geneva, intending to stay one night. The city had lately thrown off its bishop and voted to live by the gospel, under the preaching of the fiery reformer Guillaume Farel. Farel learned that the author of the Institutes was in town and came to find him. Calvin pleaded that he wanted only to study in peace. Farel answered that God would curse his quiet studies if he refused to help in so great a need. Calvin later wrote that he felt as if God had laid His hand on him from heaven. He stayed.

Expelled. The first stay did not go well. Calvin and Farel drew up articles for the ordering of the church and a confession of faith that every citizen was asked to swear to, and they insisted that the church, not the city council, must decide who came to the Lord’s Table. The councillors resisted. At Easter 1538 the ministers refused to give communion in a city they judged unready, and within days they were banished. Calvin was twenty-eight, and he was relieved.

Strasbourg. The three years that followed may have been the happiest of his life. At the urging of Martin Bucer, the wise and generous reformer of Strasbourg, he became pastor of a congregation of French refugees there. He lectured, wrote his commentary on Romans, brought out a much larger second edition of the Institutes, and answered Cardinal Sadoleto, who had written to the Genevans inviting them back to Rome. He also gathered a little book of metrical psalms for his congregation to sing. From Bucer he learned how a church could be ordered and governed. And in 1540 he married Idelette de Bure, a widow from a family of Anabaptists he had won to the Reformed faith, who came with two children of her own.

The return. Geneva, meanwhile, had fallen into disorder, and in 1540 the city begged him to come back. He dreaded it. Yet in September 1541 he returned, and there he stayed for the rest of his life. It was in writing to Farel about this summons that he used the words that became his motto: he offered his heart to the Lord, promptly and sincerely. His seal showed a hand holding out a heart.

Pastor of Geneva. Calvin never ruled Geneva. He held no civil office and became a citizen only in 1559. His power was that of the pulpit, the lecture hall and a tireless pen. Soon after his return the city adopted his Ecclesiastical Ordinances, which set out four offices in the church — pastors to preach, teachers to instruct, elders to oversee, deacons to care for the poor — and established the consistory to exercise discipline. He preached through whole books of the Bible, often every day in alternate weeks, and from 1549 a secretary took down his sermons as he spoke.

Griefs and battles. His private life was marked by loss. In 1542 Idelette bore a son, Jacques, who lived only a short time. She herself died in 1549, after long illness, and Calvin wrote to his friend Pierre Viret that he was trying to master his grief. He never remarried. His public life was a long struggle. For years, powerful Genevan families resented the consistory’s discipline and the growing numbers of French refugees, and more than once Calvin seemed near to being driven out again. His position was secured only in 1555, when his opponents were defeated after a riot.

Servetus. In the middle of these struggles came the event that has darkened his name ever since. In August 1553 Michael Servetus, a brilliant Spanish physician who had published attacks on the doctrine of the Trinity and had lately escaped from the Catholic Inquisition in France, appeared in Geneva and was recognised and arrested. Calvin drew up the articles against him. The council consulted the other Swiss churches, who agreed that he must be severely punished, and on 27 October 1553 Servetus was burned alive outside the city. Calvin had asked for a less cruel death, and was refused. He never repented of his part, and the next year he published a defence of the punishment of heretics. In 1903, Calvin’s own spiritual heirs set up a stone near the place of execution, confessing that this was an error of his age and condemning it.

The school of Christ. His last years were his most fruitful. Geneva filled with refugees from France, Italy, England, Scotland and the Netherlands, among them John Knox, who called the city the most perfect school of Christ since the days of the apostles. In 1559 Calvin founded the Genevan Academy, with Theodore Beza as its first rector, and from it trained pastors went out, many of them into danger, to plant Reformed churches across France. That same year the final edition of the Institutes appeared. In 1562 the full Genevan Psalter was completed.

How long, Lord? His health had long been broken — migraines, fevers, gout, kidney stones, and a lung disease that made him cough blood. He preached his last sermon in February 1564. In April he took leave of the city council and of the ministers, asking their forgiveness for his quick temper and thanking God for His mercy. He died on 27 May 1564. At his own request he was buried in the common cemetery without a monument, and the exact place is not known. Beza, who wrote his life, ended it by holding him up as a pattern of the Christian life, easier to slander than to imitate. Calvin would have wanted only one thing said: that God had been glorified.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Calvin tells us only that God subdued his mind and made it teachable. Write down, as simply, what God has done in your own life, and let Him be the subject of the sentence.

2. Think of a time God asked you to go somewhere you did not want to go. How did you answer? Is there such a call before you now?

3. Calvin’s happiest years came in exile. Thank God for a season of your life that looked like loss and turned out to be gift.

4. Face the story of Servetus honestly. Ask what convictions you hold so fiercely that you might be tempted to treat others without mercy for them.

5. Pray this week for a church or Christian worker in exile or under persecution, as Calvin did for the French churches all his life.

A PRAYER
Lord, You took a proud and stubborn scholar and made his mind teachable. Do the same with me.
Where You call me, give me grace to go, promptly and sincerely, even when I would rather stay in quiet.
Comfort me in loss as You comforted Your servant, and keep me faithful in long and wearisome struggles.
Forgive the sins of Your church done in Your name, and keep me from all cruelty in the defence of truth.
My heart I offer to You, O Lord. Take it, and keep it for Your glory. Amen.

fields.title: The Knowledge of God and of Ourselves
fields.body_html:
Mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes. JOB 42:5–6

The Institutes of the Christian Religion is one of the longest and most demanding books in the Christian tradition, and yet it begins with a sentence anyone can understand. Nearly all the wisdom we have, Calvin says in its opening lines, true and solid wisdom, consists of two parts: the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. Everything he goes on to write, through four books and eighty chapters, is an unfolding of that sentence. It is worth stopping on it, because it is not as obvious as it sounds.

Two kinds of knowledge bound together

The striking thing about Calvin’s opening is that he refuses to say which knowledge comes first. The two, he says in Institutes 1.1, are joined by many bonds, and it is not easy to tell which precedes and brings forth the other.

On the one hand, no one can look honestly at himself without being turned towards God. We find that our very existence is held up by Him. Every gift we have, every good thing, trickles down to us from heaven like streams from a fountain. And the other side is just as searching: our poverty, our ignorance, our emptiness and our sin remind us that true light, wisdom and goodness are found in the Lord alone. Our misery drives us to look for Him. We cannot seriously aspire to God, Calvin says, until we have begun to be displeased with ourselves.

O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me. PSALM 139:1

On the other hand, we can never come to a clear knowledge of ourselves unless we have first looked upon the face of God and then come down to look at ourselves. So long as we compare ourselves only with other people, or look no higher than the earth, we are pleased with ourselves. A man who has only ever seen black will think grey is white. It is only when we raise our eyes to God — to His holiness, His wisdom, His power — that what looked like righteousness is exposed as filth, and what looked like wisdom as folly.

Undone before the Holy One

Calvin draws his proof from Scripture. Whenever the saints of the Bible were brought into the presence of God, they were struck down and overwhelmed. He points to Job, to Abraham, who confessed himself dust and ashes, to Elijah who wrapped his face in his mantle, and above all to Isaiah in the temple.

Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts. ISAIAH 6:5

This is not self-hatred for its own sake. It is simply what happens to a creature when it sees reality. Calvin wants his readers to understand that every kind of human pride — intellectual, moral, religious — survives only in the dark. Bring it into the light of God and it withers. And that is a mercy, because the same light that humbles us is the light that heals.

For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit. ISAIAH 57:15

Knowledge that is piety

It would be easy to misunderstand what Calvin means by knowing God. He does not mean simply knowing that there is a God, or knowing correct facts about Him. In the second chapter of the Institutes he says that God is not truly known where there is no religion or piety. And he defines piety with care: it is reverence joined with love of God, which the knowledge of His benefits brings about.

That definition is the key to the whole Institutes. For Calvin the question is never merely what God is, but what He is like towards us. It is not enough to know that God exists. We must know Him as the fountain of all good, so that we look for nothing anywhere else. Until people recognise that they owe everything to God, that they are nourished by His fatherly care, that He is the author of every good thing, they will never yield Him willing service. Indeed, unless they put their whole happiness in Him, they will never give themselves to Him truly and sincerely.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction. PROVERBS 1:7

This is why Calvin distrusts idle speculation. He has no patience with people who ask what God is in Himself, while taking no interest in how He deals with us. Curiosity of that kind, he says, is cold and frivolous. The one who knows God in the right way does not invent a God to suit himself. He looks for God in His Word and His works, fears to offend Him, submits to Him as Lord and loves Him as Father, and would honour Him even if there were no hell.

The same thread in Calvin’s preaching

This conviction runs all through Calvin’s sermons. In his sermon on All Scripture Is Given by Inspiration, one of the four in the Ochorus library, he sums up the whole doctrine of the gospel in a single sentence that could have come from the opening of the Institutes: “The doctrine of the gospel, in few words, is this: to know God, and put our whole trust in him.”

Notice the pairing. To know God is to trust Him. The knowledge Calvin cares about is always a knowledge that leans its whole weight on its object. And in the same sermon he makes the other half plain: when we consider that there is nothing but sin and wickedness in us, we must learn to be displeased with ourselves. The two kinds of knowledge travel together, even in a Sunday sermon in Geneva.

But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth. JEREMIAH 9:24

A caution and a comfort

Calvin can sound severe in this opening. He speaks bluntly of our emptiness, our corruption and our misery, and a modern reader may wince. It is fair to add two things.

First, Calvin never says that human beings are worthless. Later in the Institutes he insists that we were made in the image of God, adorned with extraordinary gifts, and that even fallen human beings are to be honoured for the image they bear. His point is not that we are nothing, but that everything we have is received.

Second, the purpose of the humbling is always the comfort. Calvin brings us down only to lift us up. The person who has learned that all his good comes from God has learned where to look for all the good he still needs. The emptier we see ourselves to be, the more we are driven to the fountain that never runs dry.

For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly. PSALM 84:11

That is where the Institutes begins, and where the Christian life begins: with a glance at God and a glance at ourselves, and with the discovery that the two together send us running to Him.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Take a few minutes to list the good things in your life today. Beside each, write where it came from, and trace it back to God.

2. Ask where you have been comparing yourself with other people rather than with God, and what that comparison has done to your pride.

3. Read Isaiah 6:1–8 slowly. Notice that Isaiah’s cleansing and his calling both come after his undoing.

4. Examine your interest in God. Is it mostly curiosity about Him, or trust in Him? Turn one question you have been asking into a prayer.

5. Memorise Calvin’s sentence from his sermon: to know God, and put our whole trust in Him. Say it each morning this week.

A PRAYER
Holy Lord, when I look at myself in the light of my own opinion, I am pleased; when I look at You, I am undone.
Show me Your glory, that I may see my sin; and show me Your goodness, that I may not despair.
Teach me to know You not with a cold and curious mind, but with reverence and love, as the fountain of every good I have.
Let me put my whole trust in You, and look for nothing apart from You. Through Jesus Christ my Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Spectacles for Dim Eyes
fields.body_html:
Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. PSALM 119:105

If God has written His glory across the whole creation, why do we need a Bible? Calvin asked that question himself, and his answer is one of the best-loved images in the Institutes. Old people, he says, and those with weak sight, may be shown a beautifully written book, and they will see that there is writing on the page, but they can hardly make out two words together. Give them spectacles, and they begin to read clearly. So it is with Scripture. It gathers up the confused knowledge of God that is otherwise in our minds, scatters our darkness, and shows us plainly the true God (Institutes 1.6.1).

Why we need the spectacles

The image is modest, and its modesty is the point. Calvin does not say that creation is silent. He is sure that the world is a dazzling theatre of God’s glory, as the next chapter will show. The problem is not with the light but with our eyes. Sin has so dimmed our sight that we see the glory and yet do not see it. We turn it into idols, or into nothing at all. We need help to read what is written everywhere.

For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse. ROMANS 1:20

So God, in His kindness, did not leave us to guess. He opened His own mouth. He spoke to the patriarchs, gave His law through Moses, sent the prophets, and at last spoke by His Son, and He caused His word to be written down so that it would not be lost or corrupted. Scripture is not a rival to creation. It is the lens through which creation can be read aright, and much more besides: it alone shows us God as Redeemer in Christ.

God speaking

Behind this lies Calvin’s high view of the authority of Scripture. Its authority, he says, does not come from the church, as if the church could lend it credit. It comes from God, because God is its author. In the sermon All Scripture Is Given by Inspiration, preached on 2 Timothy 3:16, he makes the point with force. The prophets, he says, were not to be believed because Moses was a great man or Isaiah was eloquent. They were instruments in the hands of God. They spoke nothing of their own; it was God who spoke by them.

All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness. 2 TIMOTHY 3:16

He draws a searching practical conclusion. “The holy scripture will be lifeless, and without force, until we know it is God that speaketh in it.” We may read the Bible as a history of mortal men, he says, and feel nothing at all. Everything changes when we understand who is speaking. In another sermon in the Ochorus library, on Enduring Persecution for Christ, he puts the same thought more beautifully: “If we would think that in reading Scripture we are in the school of angels, we would be far more careful and desirous to profit by the doctrine which is propounded to us.”

The inner witness of the Spirit

But how do we know that God is speaking? Calvin’s answer is one of his most important contributions to Christian thought. There are good reasons to trust the Bible, he says in Institutes 1.8 — its antiquity, its majesty, the fulfilment of its prophecies, the plainness and power of its style, the way it has been preserved through persecution, the blood of the martyrs who died for it. He sets them out at length. And yet he insists that none of these proofs, on their own, can produce a settled faith. They are helps, not foundations.

The foundation is the secret witness of the Holy Spirit (Institutes 1.7). The same Spirit who spoke through the prophets must enter our hearts to persuade us that they faithfully proclaimed what God commanded. Scripture, Calvin says, is self-authenticating: it carries its own evidence, as plainly as white things show their colour or sweet things their taste. But only the Spirit can open our eyes to see it.

But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:14

This is why Calvin could be so confident without being rationalist. A believer does not need to be a scholar to be sure of God’s Word. The simple Christian reading the Gospels in her kitchen, and finding Christ speaking to her there, has the same ground of certainty as the learned doctor. In his sermon on All Scripture he calls it the infinite goodness of God, that He seals His truth in our hearts and makes us feel its power.

My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. JOHN 10:27

The whole Scripture, and nothing added

Two practical consequences follow, and Calvin presses them both hard.

First, we must receive the whole of Scripture, not just the parts we like. In the same sermon he says that “we must not pick and cull the scripture to please our own fancy, but must receive the whole without exception.” Calvin’s own ministry was the proof of his sincerity. He preached straight through book after book of the Bible, Old Testament and New, including the hard and the obscure passages, and he wrote commentaries on almost all of it.

Second, we must add nothing to it. This was the heart of Calvin’s quarrel with the church of his day. He believed that human traditions had buried the Word of God, and that consciences had been bound by rules God never gave. The sermon on All Scripture is full of sharp words against the traditions of Rome, and the modern reader will find some of them hard to hear. But the principle beneath them is sound: in matters of faith and worship, the church has no authority but that which it receives from God’s Word.

Every word of God is pure: he is a shield unto them that put their trust in him. Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar. PROVERBS 30:5–6

God stooping to speak

One more thing must be said, because it shows the tenderness beneath Calvin’s high doctrine. He believed that when God speaks to us in Scripture He accommodates Himself to our weakness. He speaks as nurses speak to little children, lisping so that we can understand (Institutes 1.13.1). He describes Himself with eyes and hands and a changing mind, not because He is like that, but because we could not grasp Him any other way. In his sermon God Will Have All Men to Be Saved Calvin says it plainly: if God should speak according to His majesty, His speech would be beyond our comprehension and would utterly confound us. The Bible is God bending down.

Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust. PSALM 103:13–14

That is why Calvin read the Bible with such reverence, and why he wanted every Christian to read it. Its purpose, as he says in the same sermon, is not to make us clever. “The word of God is not given to teach us how to talk, to make us eloquent and subtle, but to reform our lives, that the world may know we are the servants of God.”

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before you next open your Bible, stop and remind yourself who is speaking. Ask the Spirit to open your eyes.

2. Name a part of Scripture you usually avoid. Begin reading it this week, asking what God is saying there.

3. Consider where you have allowed a human rule or custom to bind your conscience as if it were God’s Word.

4. Think of a passage where God has spoken to you with unmistakable force. Thank Him for the inner witness of His Spirit.

5. Ask one honest question of your Bible reading: is it making me cleverer, or is it reforming my life?

A PRAYER
Lord God, my eyes are dim, and I cannot read Your glory rightly by myself.
Thank You for the spectacles of Your Word, and for stooping to speak to me as a father speaks to a child.
Send Your Spirit to bear witness in my heart that it is You who speak, so that I may hear with reverence and obey with joy.
Keep me from picking and choosing, and from adding my own inventions. Let Your Word reform my life, that the world may know I am Your servant. Amen.

Send Your Spirit to bear witness in my heart that it is You who speak, so that I may hear with reverence and obey with joy. Keep me from picking and choosing, and from adding my own inventions. fields.title: The Theatre of God’s Glory
fields.body_html:
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. PSALM 19:1

Calvin is often imagined as a man who could see nothing but sin. Anyone who reads the early chapters of the Institutes will find a very different writer, one who looked at the world with something like wonder. Again and again he calls the creation a theatre — a dazzling stage on which the glory of God is displayed for all to see (Institutes 1.5.8; 1.14.20). God, he says, has not only planted in our minds the seed of religion, but has so revealed Himself in the whole workmanship of the universe that we cannot open our eyes without being compelled to see Him (Institutes 1.5.1).

The seed of religion

Calvin begins with what he calls a sense of divinity. There is, he says in Institutes 1.3, an awareness of God engraved on every human mind by natural instinct. God has implanted it, so that no one can plead ignorance. Even the most distant peoples have some religion; even those who deny God most loudly are haunted by Him and tremble at the thought of judgement. The seed can be choked, but it cannot be pulled out.

Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. ROMANS 1:19

This is a remarkable conviction, and a humane one. It means that when a Christian speaks to an unbeliever about God, he is not introducing a foreign idea. He is speaking to something already there. Every person is made for God and knows, somewhere beneath the noise, that he is answerable to Him. Calvin’s sermon God Will Have All Men to Be Saved makes the same point from another angle: we must not forget that God has made us all in His own image and likeness, and that we are the workmanship of His hand.

Every corner lit with glory

From the inner sense of God Calvin turns outward, to the world. And here his prose becomes almost lyrical. The fabric of the heavens and the earth, the order of the stars, the structure of the human body with its countless marvels — all of them are marks of God’s wisdom and goodness. We do not need learning to see it. The most unlettered peasant, looking up at the night sky, cannot but see the handiwork of God, though the astronomer, Calvin says, sees more of it and has more reason to praise.

O LORD, how manifold are thy works! in wisdom hast thou made them all: the earth is full of thy riches. PSALM 104:24

He is especially struck by the human person, whom he calls, with the ancient philosophers, a little world, a mirror of God’s works. There is no need to look outside ourselves, he says; each of us carries within himself a sufficient proof of God’s power and kindness. And in the chapter on creation (Institutes 1.14) he urges believers not to hurry past the world as though it were beneath notice, but to take a pious delight in it, to contemplate God’s works with thanksgiving, and so be moved to trust, pray and praise.

I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well. PSALM 139:14

A factory of idols

Yet the theatre has an audience that will not watch. Here is the tragedy Calvin sets beside the glory. We see God’s works and we do not see God. Instead of rising from the works to their Maker, we worship the works, or worship ourselves, or invent gods in our own image. In one of his most famous observations he says that the human mind is, so to speak, a perpetual factory of idols (Institutes 1.11.8). We manufacture gods as easily as we breathe.

Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. ROMANS 1:22–23

Calvin meant this about the images and relics of the church of his day, and he was fierce against them. But the principle reaches much further. Every heart has its workshop. We shape a God who approves what we want, who asks nothing hard, who looks rather like ourselves. The glory of creation leaves us without excuse, but it does not by itself save us. That is why, as the last chapter said, we need the spectacles of Scripture, and why Calvin moves from creation to the Word.

Creation for our sake

One more strand of Calvin’s teaching on creation deserves to be heard. He loved to point out, following Genesis, that God prepared the world before He made man, as a father furnishes a house before his children arrive. Everything was ready — light, land, plants, creatures — before Adam opened his eyes. This, Calvin says, shows God’s fatherly care: He meant us to find the world full of good things, and to receive them from His hand.

And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good. GENESIS 1:31

It also means that the right use of creation is thankfulness. Later in the Institutes (3.10.2) Calvin rebukes those who would allow themselves nothing but bare necessities. God did not create food only for need, he says, but also for delight; He gave flowers their beauty and scent, and wine to gladden the heart of man. To enjoy these gifts with gratitude is not worldliness. It is to use the world as God meant.

And wine that maketh glad the heart of man, and oil to make his face to shine, and bread which strengtheneth man’s heart. PSALM 104:15

An honest word

Calvin’s picture of creation is rich, but it is not complete. He was a man of the sixteenth century, and his understanding of the natural world was that of his age. He also wrote of the created order within a strongly ordered view of society, in which each rank had its place, and not all of that belongs to the gospel. The modern reader need not share his science or his social assumptions to receive his main point: that the world is God’s, that it speaks of Him, and that we who live in it are without excuse if we do not give Him thanks.

The earth is the LORD’S, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. PSALM 24:1

Calvin’s invitation is simple. Look up. The theatre is lit. The play is being performed. Do not stare at the stage lights, and do not build your own idols in the aisles. Look to the One whose glory fills the house.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Spend ten minutes this week outdoors, looking deliberately at one part of creation. Let it lead you to praise the One who made it.

2. Consider your own body — breath, sight, the beating of your heart — as Calvin did, a little world. Give thanks for it specifically.

3. Name one idol your heart has been manufacturing: a God made to your own liking. Bring it into the light of Scripture.

4. When you next share a meal or a glass of wine with others, receive it deliberately as a gift for delight, not only for need.

5. Remember that every person you meet today bears God’s image and carries the seed of religion. Let it shape how you speak to them.

A PRAYER
Creator of heaven and earth, the whole world is the theatre of Your glory, and I have walked through it with my eyes half shut.
Open my eyes to see Your wisdom in the stars and Your kindness in my daily bread.
Break down the idols my heart keeps making, and teach me to worship You as You are, not as I would have You be.
Let me enjoy Your gifts with thankfulness, and in every gift see the Giver. Amen.

fields.title: The Fatherly Hand
fields.body_html:
Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. MATTHEW 10:29–30

To make God the Creator, Calvin says, and then leave Him idle, would be cold and barren. Many people believe that God made the world once and then left it to run by itself, like a clockmaker who winds the clock and walks away. Faith, Calvin insists, must go further. It must see God not only as the One who made all things, but as the One who governs and sustains them, down to the least sparrow (Institutes 1.16.1). This is the doctrine of providence, and for Calvin it was not a puzzle for philosophers but one of the chief comforts of the Christian life.

No such thing as chance

Calvin’s teaching is bold. Nothing happens by chance. Not only the great movements of history, but the smallest events — a branch falling, a traveller meeting robbers, a sailor lost at sea — are governed by God’s secret counsel. He rejects the idea that God simply watches over a world that moves by its own laws, and the idea that He directs things in general but leaves the details to fortune. God rules all things, great and small, and He rules them for His purposes.

The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD. PROVERBS 16:33

He is careful to add that this does not make God the author of evil. Wicked people do real wickedness, and they are guilty of it; God uses even their malice for His own good ends, as He used the brothers of Joseph and the crucifiers of Christ, without being stained by their sin.

But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. GENESIS 50:20

Nor does providence make human effort pointless. Calvin is scornful of those who say that if everything is fixed there is no need to take care. God, he says in Institutes 1.17.4, who has set the bounds of our life, has also entrusted us with its care, given us means to preserve it, and warned us of dangers so that we may avoid them. We must use means, plan wisely, take medicine when we are ill. We simply do not trust the means. We trust the God who works through them.

An impregnable fortress

What makes Calvin’s doctrine of providence so warm is the use he makes of it. In Institutes 1.17 he paints a vivid picture of human life without it. Our body, he says, is the receptacle of a thousand diseases. We cannot go on a ship without being a step from death, or mount a horse without risking a fall, or walk down a street without danger from falling tiles. Fire, wild beasts, robbers, the weather — all threaten us. If we believed the world ran by chance, we would be sunk in endless anxiety.

The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust. PSALM 18:2

But once the light of providence has shone on a godly person, he is relieved not only of that extreme anxiety but of every care. He knows that his heavenly Father holds all things in His power, that no creature can move except by His will, and that he is under the Father’s protection. Calvin says that ignorance of providence is the greatest of all miseries, and the knowledge of it the highest blessedness.

He preached the same comfort to his people in his sermon on Enduring Persecution for Christ, in the Ochorus library. Speaking to believers who might face prison or the stake, he told them that God “is not divested of the guardianship which He exercises over their persons,” and that “His providence, as He unfolds it, ought to be regarded by us as an impregnable fortress.” Not a hair, he says, will be plucked from their heads without His leave.

Patience, gratitude and freedom from fear

Calvin draws three practical fruits from this teaching (Institutes 1.17.7–11).

The first is patience in adversity. When trouble comes, the believer does not rage against men or curse his luck. He remembers that it comes from the hand of God, and he looks to the purpose behind it. He can say with Job that the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.

The LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. JOB 1:21

The second is gratitude in prosperity. Every good thing that comes to us, even through the kindness of other people, is to be received as coming from God. We thank the human helper, but we see the divine hand behind him.

The third is freedom from anxiety about the future. The one who knows that God holds tomorrow need not be tormented by it. This is not a stoic indifference. Calvin was no stoic; he felt his griefs keenly and says so. It is a child’s confidence in a Father.

Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God. PHILIPPIANS 4:6

The hard places

Calvin’s doctrine of providence raises real difficulties, and it is only fair to name them. If God governs everything, how is He not responsible for evil? Calvin answers by distinguishing God’s secret will from His revealed will, and by insisting that God acts justly even where we cannot see how. He admits that there is a depth here we cannot plumb, and he warns against prying into it.

Many readers will find that answer incomplete, and some will feel that Calvin at times presses God’s control so hard that human freedom and the reality of evil seem to shrink. That tension is real, and it runs through the whole Bible, which teaches both that God rules all things and that human beings are responsible for what they do. Calvin holds both, even if he leans heavily on the first. The wise reader will hold both as well, and will be slow to explain a particular suffering as though he had read God’s secret counsel. Calvin himself says that we must not ask for reasons God has not given.

The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever. DEUTERONOMY 29:29

What no reader should lose is the comfort at the centre. The world is not in the hands of chance, or fate, or the powerful. It is in the hands of a Father.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name the fear that most often keeps you awake. Bring it deliberately under the truth that your Father holds all things.

2. Recall a hard event in your past. Ask not why it happened, but how God has used it, and give thanks for what you can see.

3. Thank one person this week for a kindness they did you, and then thank God who sent it through them.

4. Examine whether you have been neglecting means — prudence, medicine, planning — out of a false trust, or trusting the means more than God.

5. When you hear of a disaster, resist explaining it. Pray instead for those who suffer, and rest in the God who rules.

A PRAYER
Heavenly Father, not a sparrow falls without You, and the hairs of my head are numbered.
Deliver me from the anxiety of those who believe the world is ruled by chance, and make Your providence my fortress.
In adversity give me patience, in prosperity give me gratitude, and for the future give me a quiet heart.
Where I cannot understand Your ways, teach me to trust Your hand, for it is the hand of my Father. Through Jesus Christ. Amen.

fields.title: A Will in Bondage
fields.body_html:
The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? JEREMIAH 17:9

The second book of the Institutes opens with a warning. There is a kind of self-knowledge, Calvin says, that is flattering and deadly: the kind that dwells on our gifts and our dignity and leaves us swollen with pride. There is another kind that is humbling and wholesome, and it is the one we need. We must know what we were made to be, and we must know what we have become (Institutes 2.1.1–3). Only then will we despair of ourselves and look for help where it can be found.

What we were, and what we are

Calvin never begins with our sin. He begins with our glory. Adam was created in the image of God, with a clear mind, an upright will and every faculty ordered towards his Maker. That, Calvin says, is our true nobility. We should remember it, not to be proud of it, but to grieve over what we lost.

So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. GENESIS 1:27

And we lost it through pride. Calvin sees the root of Adam’s fall not simply in eating forbidden fruit, but in unbelief — refusing to trust God’s Word — and in the ambition to be more than a creature. From that one act came the ruin of the whole race. He is free to do what he loves; he is not free to love what he should.

This was why Calvin disliked the phrase free will. He did not object to the idea that human beings make real choices. Take away my heart of stone and give me a heart of flesh. Make my unwilling will willing, and heal what I have broken.
Whatever good is in me, let me confess it as Your gift, and give You all the glory. Through Jesus Christ. Amen.

fields.title: The Mediator, God and Man
fields.body_html:
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. 1 TIMOTHY 2:5

Everything in the first book of the Institutes leads to a closed door. God is glorious, the world is His theatre, and we are without excuse; but we are sinners, our wills are in bondage, and the law only condemns us. How can such creatures come near such a God? Calvin’s answer, in the second book, is a Person. The knowledge of God the Creator is not enough; we must know Him as Redeemer, and He is known as Redeemer only in Christ the Mediator (Institutes 2.6.1).

God manifest in the flesh

Calvin preached on the great text of 1 Timothy 3:16, and his sermon The Mystery of Godliness is in the Ochorus library. It is one of the finest things he wrote on the person of Christ.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. 1 TIMOTHY 3:16

He begins in astonishment. That God should become man, he says, so far surpasses our understanding that when we are told of it we are astonished. Who is the Lord of glory, that He should humble Himself so far as to be joined to us, take the form of a servant, and even suffer the curse that was due to us? The living God, the well-spring of life, the everlasting glory, has not only come near our misery, but been joined to it and made one with it, in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Why must the Mediator be God? Because, as Calvin argues in the sermon and in Institutes 2.12, no mere creature could bear the weight of our salvation. Only God could conquer death, overcome sin and give life. We could not trust in Christ at all unless He were God, since Scripture curses the one who trusts in man.

And why must He be man? Because it was in our nature that sin was committed, and in our nature it had to be answered. Only a man could obey in our place and die in our place. And only as a man could He become our brother, so that we can come to God familiarly in His name. In the sermon Calvin draws both truths together in a single sentence: “Let us so distinguish the two natures which are in him, that we may know that the Son of God is our brother.”

Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same; that through death he might destroy him that had the power of death, that is, the devil. HEBREWS 2:14

Two natures, one person

Calvin was deeply concerned to keep the old doctrine of the church about Christ: that He is one person in two natures, truly God and truly man, without confusion and without division. In the sermon he uses a homely picture. We have two eyes, each with its own office; but when we look steadily at something, our two sights are joined and become one. So there are two different natures in Christ, and yet He is one.

He also warns that the mystery must be approached humbly. “Pride hath always been the mother of heresies,” he says. When we hear the word mystery, we should learn to keep our minds in check, and at the same time to climb up beyond ourselves and reverence a majesty that passes understanding.

Prophet, priest and king

In Institutes 2.15 Calvin gave the church one of its most lasting ways of describing the work of Christ. He is our prophet, our priest and our king. These three offices had been given in the Old Testament to different people, each anointed for the task. In Christ, the Anointed One, they are all fulfilled together.

As prophet, Christ is the final and perfect teacher of the Father’s will. All the prophets pointed to Him; in Him God has spoken His last word. We must not look for any wisdom beyond His.

God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son. HEBREWS 1:1–2

As king, He rules His church and His people, not with outward pomp but by His Word and Spirit. His kingdom is spiritual, Calvin says, and its benefits reach to eternal life. Because He reigns, we can endure every hardship of this life with patience, knowing that our King will never leave us defenceless and will bring us through to the end.

As priest, He reconciles us to God by His sacrifice and intercedes for us still. This is the heart of the matter.

The price of our peace

In Institutes 2.16 Calvin sets out Christ’s work as priest with great tenderness. We were enemies of God, under His just wrath. And yet — Calvin insists — God did not begin to love us because Christ died; He sent Christ because He already loved us. The cross does not change God’s heart. It reveals it, and it deals with the barrier of our guilt that stood between us and His love.

But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. ROMANS 5:8

Christ, Calvin says, took our place. He stood before the judge as a criminal, was condemned though innocent, and bore the curse that belonged to us, so that we might be set free. He was, as Calvin puts it in The Mystery of Godliness, as it were accursed of God the Father when He offered Himself a sacrifice, that through Him we might be blessed.

Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree. GALATIANS 3:13

Calvin also gave a distinctive reading of the phrase in the Creed, he descended into hell. He understood it to mean that Christ suffered in His soul the dreadful torments of a condemned and forsaken man — the agony of Gethsemane and the cry from the cross (Institutes 2.16.10). Not every reader has followed him in taking the words of the Creed this way, and it is fair to say that this is his own interpretation. But the truth behind it is profound: Christ did not only die the death of the body. He endured in His soul the separation from God that our sin deserved.

Brother and Lord

The warmest note in Calvin’s teaching about Christ is that we may come to Him as a brother without ever ceasing to worship Him as God. In The Mystery of Godliness he says that we may come to Him as our brother, and at the same time worship Him as the everlasting God by whom we were made and are preserved. Both belong together. A Christ who was only God would be too far away to reach. A Christ who was only man could not save us.

Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession. HEBREWS 4:14
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read 1 Timothy 3:16 slowly several times, and let yourself be astonished that God was manifest in the flesh.

2. Ask which of Christ’s three offices you most neglect: do you listen to Him as prophet, trust Him as priest, obey Him as king?

3. Remember that God did not begin to love you because Christ died; Christ died because God loved you. Let that settle any fear that God is reluctant.

4. Pray this week in Christ’s name deliberately, remembering that you come to the Father as a brother or sister of the Son.

5. Where you have tried to understand the mystery of Christ proudly, ask for humility, and worship where you cannot comprehend.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man, You humbled Yourself to be joined to us in our flesh, and to bear the curse that was ours.
Be my prophet, and teach me; be my priest, and cleanse me; be my king, and rule me.
Let me never forget that You are my brother, nor ever cease to worship You as my God.
I bow before a mystery I cannot fathom, and I thank You for a love I did not deserve. Amen.

fields.title: Engrafted into Christ
fields.body_html:
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing. JOHN 15:5

Calvin’s third book begins with a question that is easy to skip and impossible to overstate. Christ has done everything necessary for our salvation. He has obeyed, suffered, died and risen. But how does what He did become ours? How do His benefits reach us? Calvin’s answer, at the head of Institutes 3.1, is one of the most important sentences he ever wrote. As long as Christ remains outside us, and we are separated from Him, all that He suffered and did for the salvation of the human race remains useless and of no value to us. To share with us what He has received from the Father, He had to become ours and dwell within us.

Union with Christ

This is the doctrine of union with Christ, and many students of Calvin have come to see it as the key to his whole account of salvation. Christ is not a distant benefactor who hands us gifts from afar. He gives Himself, and all His gifts come with Him. We are engrafted into Him, as a branch into a tree, so that His life flows into us.

For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. GALATIANS 3:27

Calvin says this is the work of the Holy Spirit. The Spirit is the bond by which Christ effectually unites us to Himself. The Son of God is in heaven; we are on earth; the Spirit joins what distance would separate. And the Spirit does it chiefly by giving faith, which Calvin calls the principal work of the Spirit (Institutes 3.1.4).

But he that is joined unto the Lord is one spirit. 1 CORINTHIANS 6:17

The same truth runs through the sermons in the Ochorus library. In The Mystery of Godliness Calvin says: “We have no faith, if we know not that our Lord Jesus Christ is joined to us, that we may become his members.” And he adds that Christ “was pleased to join himself to us, that we might be partakers of his substance.” In God Will Have All Men to Be Saved he describes the moment of calling in the same language: God touches us with His Holy Spirit, and we are grafted, as it were, into the body of our Lord Jesus Christ; and this, he says, is the true earnest of our adoption.

The double grace

From union with Christ flow two great gifts, which Calvin calls a double grace (Institutes 3.11.1). By partaking of Christ we receive, first, that we are reconciled to God through His blamelessness, so that we have in heaven a gracious Father instead of a judge. And second, that we are sanctified by His Spirit, so that we may cultivate blamelessness and purity of life.

But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:30

The first gift is justification: God counts us righteous for Christ’s sake. The second is sanctification: God makes us holy by His Spirit. The two are distinct, and Calvin will not allow them to be confused. We are not justified because we are being made holy; we are justified freely, by grace, for the sake of Christ alone. But neither will he allow them to be separated. You cannot have Christ for justification without having Him for sanctification. He is not divided.

In a striking image, Calvin compares the two to the light and heat of the sun (Institutes 3.11.6). The sun warms the earth by its heat and lights it by its brightness. The two are inseparable, yet the light is not the heat, and the heat is not the light. So it is with the double grace.

Why the order matters

Calvin made a surprising choice in arranging the Institutes. Before he writes about justification by faith, the great doctrine of the Reformation, he writes at length about repentance and the Christian life. Only afterwards does he turn to justification. Some readers have been puzzled by this. Why not begin with the forgiveness of sins?

Calvin explains his reasons himself (Institutes 3.11.1). He wanted to show from the outset that the faith by which we are freely justified is never idle or empty of good works. Rome accused the Reformers of teaching that faith alone makes holiness unnecessary. Calvin answers by showing, before anything else, that those united to Christ are always being changed by Him.

The beauty of this teaching is that it keeps Christ at the centre of everything. It is not that Christ earns forgiveness for us and then leaves us to do the rest. He Himself is our righteousness and our holiness. He is both for us and in us.

The language of union with Christ can be misused. Thank You that in You I am a child of God and an heir of all You have. Amen.

fields.body_html:
Now faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen. HEBREWS 11:1

If union with Christ is the way His benefits reach us, faith is the hand by which we receive Him. So Calvin devotes one of the longest chapters of the Institutes (3.2) to the question of what faith is. It is a chapter every Christian would profit from reading, because Calvin clears away a great deal of confusion that still clouds the subject.

What faith is not

He begins by saying what faith is not. It is not mere assent to the teachings of the church. In his day many people were told that it was enough to believe whatever the church believed, even if they did not know what that was. Calvin calls this implicit faith and dismisses it. Faith, he says, does not rest on ignorance but on knowledge — knowledge not only of God but of God’s will towards us.

Nor is faith simply believing that God exists, or that the Bible is true, or that Christ died. The devils believe all of that, and tremble. A person may know the whole history of the gospel and still not have faith in the biblical sense.

Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. JAMES 2:19

Calvin’s definition

Then comes the definition, one of the most carefully built sentences in the Institutes (3.2.7). Faith, Calvin says in substance, is a firm and certain knowledge of God’s kindness towards us, founded on the truth of the free promise in Christ, revealed to our minds and sealed upon our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

Every part of that definition matters.

Faith is knowledge. It has content. It knows something true. But Calvin quickly adds that this is not the kind of knowledge we have of things we can see and measure. It is more like being persuaded than comprehending. We are sure of what we cannot fully grasp.

It is firm and certain. Calvin will have nothing of a faith that always hovers in doubt. God wants His children to be sure of His love.

Its object is God’s kindness, His benevolence, towards us. Faith is not only believing that God is, but believing that He is for us. It is knowing Him as a Father.

It is founded on the free promise in Christ. Faith does not rest on our feelings, our experiences or our goodness. It rests on what God has said, and above all on the promise of mercy in His Son. Faith and the Word belong together, Calvin says, as a building belongs to its foundation.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

And it is revealed to the mind and sealed on the heart by the Spirit. Faith is not merely a matter of the head. The Spirit must enlighten the mind to understand the promise, and then confirm it in the heart so that we trust it. Calvin says that it is harder for the heart to be assured than for the mind to be instructed.

Assurance and doubt

One of the most pastorally important things Calvin teaches here concerns assurance. He believed that faith, by its nature, includes a certain confidence that God is gracious to me. He did not think of assurance as a rare privilege reserved for a few advanced saints.

For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. ROMANS 8:38–39

But — and this is what makes him wise rather than naive — he also insists that faith in this life is always mixed with doubt (Institutes 3.2.17–18). Believers are never wholly free from unbelief. They are tossed about, shaken and troubled. The flesh fights against the spirit. What distinguishes true faith is not the absence of doubt but that faith, however hard pressed, always rises again. Like the psalmist, the believer argues with his own soul and hopes in God again.

Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. PSALM 42:11

Calvin compares faith to a man in a dark prison who sees the sun only through a narrow window, slanting and partial. He sees little of it, but he is not deceived: it is really the sun, and its light is real. So the weakest believer truly sees God’s kindness in Christ, however dimly.

Faith that is always about Christ

The deepest point in Calvin’s teaching on faith is that it always looks to Christ. We cannot trust God’s general goodness in the abstract; our sins would make us afraid of Him. We can trust Him only where He has shown Himself gracious, and that is in His Son. Christ is the mirror in which we see the Father’s love.

In his sermon on Enduring Persecution for Christ, Calvin insists that the firmness a believer needs in suffering cannot come from anything else. “The firmness necessary we can not possess, unless it be founded on certainty of faith.” To hazard our life on a guess, he says, would be rashness, not Christian courage. The martyrs could go to the fire because they knew whom they had believed.

For the which cause I also suffer these things: nevertheless I am not ashamed: for I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that he is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. 2 TIMOTHY 1:12

Faith and love

Calvin did not deny that true faith always works by love. But he was careful not to make love part of the definition of faith, as the medieval theologians had done, because he feared it would turn faith back into a kind of work. Faith receives; it does not pay. Love, holiness and good works flow from it, as fruit from a tree, but they are not the root of our acceptance.

For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love. GALATIANS 5:6

A caution

Calvin’s high view of assurance has sometimes been heard, by tender consciences, as a demand: if you are not perfectly sure, you have no faith at all. That is not what he meant, and his own teaching on the conflict of faith and doubt should prevent it. Later Reformed writers spent many pages helping troubled believers who lacked assurance. Calvin’s point is that assurance belongs to faith’s nature, not that every believer feels it equally at every moment. The one who clings to Christ in the dark still has the sun, though only through a narrow window.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write out Calvin’s definition of faith in your own words, and pray through each part of it.

2. Ask what your faith rests on at present: feelings, experiences, your own progress, or God’s promise in Christ.

3. Find one promise of God in Scripture that speaks directly to your present need, and resolve to stand on it.

4. If doubt is troubling you, do not be ashamed. Read Psalm 42 aloud, and let faith argue with your soul.

5. Thank God for the certainty the martyrs had, and ask Him to root your own faith as deeply.

A PRAYER
Father, I cannot trust You by looking at myself; I can trust You only where You have shown Yourself gracious, in Jesus Christ.
Open my mind to understand Your promise, and seal it on my heart by Your Spirit, so that I know You are for me.
When doubt shakes me, lift me again. Let me see Your kindness, even if only through a narrow window.
Root my faith in Your Word, so that I may be firm in trouble and not ashamed of Your name. Amen.

fields.title: Repentance the Whole Life Long
fields.body_html:
Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me. PSALM 51:10

Luther’s first thesis, nailed to the church door in 1517, said that when our Lord Jesus Christ called us to repent, He willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. Calvin agreed completely, and in Institutes 3.3 he set out what that means. Repentance is not a single moment at the start of the Christian life, nor a sacrament to be performed when conscience troubles us. It is the shape of the whole life of a believer, from conversion to the grave.

Repentance flows from faith

Calvin makes a point here that surprised some of his readers. Repentance, he says, does not come before faith, as if we had to reform ourselves before we could believe. It is born of faith (Institutes 3.3.1). Of course the preaching of repentance and the preaching of faith go together, and a sinner is often first awakened by fear of judgement. But true repentance — a heart turned to God in love — is possible only for the one who already knows that God is merciful. No one can seriously turn to God unless he knows God to be gracious.

But there is forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared. PSALM 130:4

This protects repentance from becoming a work by which we try to earn forgiveness. We do not repent in order to make God kind. We repent because He is kind.

Dying and rising

Calvin defines repentance as the true turning of our life to God, a turning that arises from a sincere and earnest fear of Him, and that consists in the mortifying of our flesh and the old man, and the quickening of the Spirit (Institutes 3.3.5). Mortification and vivification — a dying and a coming alive. Both come from our participation in Christ. Because we are united to Him in His death, the old self is put to death; because we are united to Him in His resurrection, we are raised to newness of life.

Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin. ROMANS 6:6

Calvin’s word for the goal of this is regeneration, the restoring of the image of God in us that was defaced by sin. It does not happen in a moment, or a day, or a year. God wipes out the corruption of the flesh little by little, and cleanses His children throughout their whole lives.

But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord. 2 CORINTHIANS 3:18

Sin remains, but does not reign

This leads to one of Calvin’s most realistic teachings. Believers are not made perfect in this life. Sin remains in them, and it is still truly sin, not merely weakness. There will always be a battle. But sin no longer reigns. It dwells in the believer, but it no longer has dominion (Institutes 3.3.10–11).

For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. GALATIANS 5:17

This saves the Christian from two dangers. It saves him from despair when he finds sin still in himself, because he knows this is the normal condition of a believer on earth. And it saves him from complacency, because he knows that every remaining sin must be fought.

The fruits of repentance

What does repentance look like in practice? Calvin answers that its fruits are the duties of love and holiness towards God and our neighbour, and a sincere purity of life. He was suspicious of outward shows — fasting, weeping, penances — when they were taken as the substance of repentance rather than its signs. The inward turning of the heart is what God looks for.

And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness. JOEL 2:13

Much of Institutes 3.4 and 3.5 is taken up with a long argument against the medieval system of penance: private confession to a priest as necessary for forgiveness, satisfactions to be paid for sins, indulgences and purgatory. Calvin’s objection was that all of these, in their different ways, made forgiveness depend on something other than the finished work of Christ. His polemic is heated, and a modern reader need not share its tone. But his central concern is pastoral: a troubled sinner must be sent straight to Christ, not to a list of tasks.

He did not despise confession. He thought it good to confess our sins to God first, and also, when it helps, to a pastor or a fellow believer, for counsel and comfort, and to confess openly when we have wronged someone or given public offence. What he opposed was making it a law and a condition of pardon.

The law as a guide

Here the third use of the law, mentioned earlier in this book, comes into its own. For the believer, Calvin says, the law is no longer a curse. It is the best instrument for learning daily what the will of the Lord is. And it is a spur to a sluggish heart, as a whip to an idle and balky ass, as he rather unflatteringly puts it (Institutes 2.7.12). The believer delights in the law because it shows him how to please the God who has saved him.

O how love I thy law! it is my meditation all the day. PSALM 119:97

Calvin preached the same thing in his sermon on All Scripture. The Scripture, he says, is profitable for correction as well as doctrine. It is not enough for us to be shown what is good; we are so cold that we hardly notice it, and God must stir us up. We must be willing to be reproved, and not look for a teacher who will only flatter us.

A gentle word

Calvin’s teaching on repentance is bracing, and it can be heard as endless self-examination. It is worth remembering that he intended it as good news. The same Spirit who shows us our sin is the Spirit of adoption. The dying is always for the sake of the rising. A Christian who repents daily is not a Christian in constant fear, but one who returns daily to a Father who is always glad to receive him.
