fields.body_html:
What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God’s. 1 CORINTHIANS 6:19–20

In the middle of the Institutes, between the chapters on repentance and on justification, Calvin placed five short chapters on the Christian life (3.6–10). They are so warm and practical that they were soon printed separately, and they have been read on their own ever since, often under the title The Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life. If you read nothing else of Calvin, read these. And at their heart is the chapter on self-denial, which begins with some of the finest lines he ever wrote.

Whose we are

Calvin builds the whole chapter on Paul’s words: ye are not your own. We are not our own, he says (Institutes 3.7.1); therefore let neither our reason nor our will sway our plans and deeds. We are not our own; therefore let us not set it as our goal to seek what is expedient for us according to the flesh. We are not our own; therefore let us, as far as we can, forget ourselves and all that is ours.

And then he turns it round. We are God’s; let us therefore live for Him and die for Him. We are God’s; let His wisdom and will rule all our actions. We are God’s; let every part of our life strive towards Him as our only lawful goal.

For none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself. For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord’s. ROMANS 14:7–8

The rhythm of that passage is the rhythm of Calvin’s own life. It is his motto — the heart offered promptly and sincerely — turned into a rule for every believer. He had wanted a quiet life among his books, and he gave it up because he was not his own. What he asked of his readers he had first asked of himself.

Self-denial towards God

Calvin says that self-denial has two sides: one towards God, the other towards our neighbours. Towards God it means surrendering our plans, our wishes and our judgement to His will. It means seeking His glory rather than our own. The greatest enemy here, Calvin says, is self-love, which lies hidden deep in every heart and turns even our good works into a kind of display.

Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. MATTHEW 16:24

It also means accepting whatever God sends. In Institutes 3.7.8–10 Calvin writes that the believer will not seek wealth, honour or success by any means that God forbids, nor count on his own skill and effort to obtain them. He will commit his plans to God, and if things do not go as he hoped, he will bear it with a quiet mind, because he knows that it is God who gives and withholds. This, says Calvin, is the only way to be at peace in a world of constant change.

Self-denial towards our neighbour

The second side of self-denial is towards other people, and here Calvin is at his most searching. Every one of us, he says, thinks himself superior to others. We flatter our own gifts and belittle theirs. We are quick to notice the faults of others and slow to notice our own. Self-denial means humbling ourselves before one another, honouring the gifts of God in others, and seeking their good rather than our own.

Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. PHILIPPIANS 2:3

Then comes one of the most remarkable passages in the whole Institutes (3.7.6). Scripture tells us to do good to all people. But many of them, Calvin says, are unworthy — by their own merits they deserve nothing from us. How then can we love them? Calvin answers that we must not look at what they deserve, but at the image of God in them, which deserves all our honour and love. Is someone a stranger? The Lord has given him a mark that ought to be familiar to you. Is he contemptible and worthless? The Lord shows him to be one whom He has honoured with His image. Has he wronged you? Remember not his malice but the image of God in him, which covers and blots out his offences.

But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you. MATTHEW 5:44

This is Calvin at his best, and it is worth setting beside the harshness that marked some of his public life. The same man who could be so severe with opponents wrote that we must love even those who hate us, for the sake of the image they bear. The reader is entitled to hold him to his own teaching.

Stewards, not owners

Calvin draws another practical rule from this. Whatever gifts we have, he says, we hold as stewards, and we will have to give account of them (Institutes 3.7.5). The only right use of every gift is to share it freely and kindly with others. He compares the church to a body, in which no member keeps its strength for itself but uses it for the whole. The Christian who is rich, gifted or strong has these things not for himself but for his neighbour.

As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. 1 PETER 4:10

This was not theory in Geneva. Calvin’s city was full of refugees, and he pressed the prosperous to give generously for their relief. A later chapter of this book will describe that work.

Freedom in surrender

It might seem that such self-denial would crush the human spirit. Calvin believed the opposite. The person who belongs to himself is a slave to his own desires, anxious, restless and never satisfied. The person who knows he is God’s is free. He does not have to manage his own destiny, defend his own glory, or secure his own future. Those are in better hands.

For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. MATTHEW 16:25
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Calvin’s chapter on self-denial (Institutes 3.7) this week; it is short and among the best things he wrote.

2. Say to yourself each morning: I am not my own. Then ask what that means for one decision you face today.

3. Think of someone you find hard to love. Look for the image of God in them, and do them one practical kindness.

4. List your gifts — money, time, skill, strength — and ask how each could be used for others rather than yourself.

5. Name a plan that has failed or been frustrated. Commit it to God and ask for a quiet mind about it.

A PRAYER
Lord, I am not my own. I was bought with a price, and I belong to You in body and spirit.
Root out the self-love that hides in my heart and spoils even my good works.
Teach me to see Your image in every person, even those who wrong me, and to love them for Your sake.
Make me a faithful steward of all You have given me, and set me free by the surrender of myself to You. Amen.

fields.title: Bearing the Cross
fields.body_html:
Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach. HEBREWS 13:13

Calvin wrote about suffering as a man who knew it. He lived as a refugee for most of his adult life. He buried his only son and his wife. He was ill for years with painful diseases. And he pastored a city full of exiles, and wrote constantly to believers in France who were in prison or facing death for the gospel. When he says in Institutes 3.8 that the Christian must bear the cross, he is not speaking from a comfortable study.

The cross belongs to the Christian life

The chapter begins by saying that the godly mind must rise higher still than self-denial, to where Christ calls every disciple to take up his cross. Those whom the Lord has adopted and deemed worthy of His fellowship ought to prepare themselves for a hard, toilsome and restless life, full of many and various kinds of evil. It is the Father’s will to exercise His children in this way (Institutes 3.8.1).

Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution. 2 TIMOTHY 3:12

Calvin’s reason is Christ Himself. If the Son of God, whom the Father loved above all, was treated this way, why should we expect to be spared? And he adds a comfort: by sharing Christ’s sufferings, we share also in His resurrection. The cross is the road, not the destination.

He preached the same in his sermon on Enduring Persecution for Christ, in the Ochorus library, taken from the words of Hebrews 13:13. There he says plainly that “there are two things which can not be separated,” namely “to be members of Christ, and to be tried by many afflictions.” And he pictures the Christian as a soldier always ready: “a Christian, even in repose, must always have one foot lifted to march to battle.”

Why God sends the cross

Calvin gives several reasons why God lays the cross on His children, and each of them is worth weighing.

First, to humble us. We are all inclined to trust our own strength. When things go well, we imagine we are invincible. God sends trouble to show us how weak we really are, and to teach us to lean on Him alone (Institutes 3.8.2).

Second, to prove and strengthen our faith and patience. Calvin often uses the image of gold refined in the fire, which he also uses in the sermon: if gold and silver, which are only corruptible metals, are tested by fire, it is reasonable that our faith, which is worth more than all the riches of the world, should be tried too.

That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. 1 PETER 1:7

Third, to correct us. Some of our troubles are the Father’s discipline, meant to call us back when we stray. Calvin insists that this is the chastening of a father, not the punishment of a judge.

For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth. HEBREWS 12:6

Fourth, and most honourably, some suffering is persecution for righteousness’ sake. To suffer for the gospel, Calvin says, is a special mark of God’s favour. In the sermon he asks who we are, poor worms of the earth, full of vanity, that God should use us as witnesses to His truth — an honour, he says, that does not even belong to the angels.

Not a stoic

One of the most humane things in Calvin’s teaching on the cross is his rejection of stoicism (Institutes 3.8.9). The Stoic philosophers taught that the wise man should feel no grief. Calvin thought this was neither possible nor Christian. Christ Himself groaned and wept, and was troubled in spirit. We are not asked to be unfeeling. We are asked to bear our grief with patience and to submit to God in the midst of it.

Jesus wept. JOHN 11:35

In the sermon he admits the same honestly: “it is only too natural for us to shun the cross.” Prophets and apostles, he says, went to death not without feeling some inclination to recoil. The flesh rebels. What matters is that the will of God has the mastery in the end. We may weep; we must not rebel.

This is the kind of patience that fits a man who, after his wife’s death, told a friend that he was trying to master his grief. He did not pretend it did not hurt.

Courage from the promises

The sermon on Enduring Persecution is a powerful piece of pastoral encouragement for believers who might be arrested at any time, and it contains Calvin’s most concrete comforts for the suffering. He sets out three promises. First, God holds our life and death in His hand, and nothing can happen to us without His leave. Second, God will sustain us by His Spirit so that our enemies gain no real advantage. Third, our suffering will bear fruit, and we will be gathered with Christ into His glory.

He tells, too, of a young man who had lived in Geneva and was arrested at Tournai. He was told he would be beheaded if he recanted and burned alive if he did not. When asked what he meant to do, he answered: “He who will give me grace to die patiently for His name, will surely give me grace to bear the fire.” Calvin tells his hearers to take that as the voice of the Holy Spirit.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. 2 CORINTHIANS 12:9

And he offers one of the tenderest sentences in all his sermons, drawn from Christ’s words to Saul on the Damascus road, that He Himself is persecuted in His members: “Jesus Christ must forget Himself before He can cease to think of us when we are in prison, or in danger of death for His cause.”

A word of honesty

It must be said that Calvin, who wrote so movingly for persecuted believers, was himself party to the persecution of Servetus. He saw no contradiction, because he believed Servetus was a blasphemer and not a witness to truth; in the sermon he is careful to distinguish true martyrs from those who die for their own absurd opinions. Few Christians today would accept that the state should put anyone to death for heresy. The reader may take Calvin’s comfort for the persecuted with gratitude, and turn it, as he did not, into a reason never to persecute.

Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 5:10
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name the cross you are carrying at present. Ask which of Calvin’s purposes God may be working through it.

2. Do not pretend. If you are grieving, tell God so honestly, and then ask for patience to submit to Him in it.

3. Pray by name this week for Christians who are in prison or in danger for their faith.

4. Ask whether you are ready, as Calvin says, with one foot lifted — prepared to be put to some cost for Christ.

5. Examine whether you have ever made others suffer for their convictions, and ask forgiveness where you have.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You bore the cross for me, and You call me to follow You and bear mine.
When trouble comes, humble my pride, refine my faith, and correct me as a Father corrects a child.
Let me weep without rebelling and suffer without despair, knowing that my life and death are in Your hand.
Strengthen Your persecuted people everywhere, and keep me from ever causing others to suffer for Your name. Amen.

fields.title: Meditation on the Future Life
fields.body_html:
If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth. COLOSSIANS 3:1–2

The third of Calvin’s chapters on the Christian life (Institutes 3.9) has a title that sounds old-fashioned: meditation on the future life. Most modern Christians do not meditate on heaven much. We are busy, and heaven feels far away. Calvin thought that was precisely the problem, and his chapter is a remedy for it.

Why God sends troubles

He begins by linking this chapter to the last. Whatever kind of trouble presses on us, he says, we must always look to this end: to accustom ourselves to despise the present life and to be roused to meditate on the future life (Institutes 3.9.1). God knows how strongly we are inclined to love this world with a blind and brutish love. So He sends troubles to loosen our grip on it. When we are full of health, wealth and success, we settle down here as if we would live for ever. When our plans fail and our comforts are taken away, we remember that we are pilgrims.

For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. HEBREWS 13:14

This is one of the most practical things Calvin says about suffering. Our afflictions are not random. They are the Father gently weaning His children from a world that cannot satisfy them, so that they will long for their true home.

These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. HEBREWS 11:13

Contempt without ingratitude

Calvin speaks strongly of despising the present life, and a modern reader may flinch. Is he saying that this world is worthless? No. He is careful to add at once that the contempt he means must never become hatred of life or ingratitude to God (Institutes 3.9.3). This life, he says, however full of misery, is still to be counted among the blessings of God. In it we begin to taste His kindness. In it He trains us for the kingdom. It is a gift, and we must receive it with thanks.

This is the day which the LORD hath made; we will rejoice and be glad in it. PSALM 118:24

What Calvin means is a comparison. Set beside the life to come, the present life is small. The mistake is not to value this life but to value it as if it were everything. When we weigh it against heaven, we can hold it loosely — not because it is nothing, but because what is coming is so much more.

Longing for the day

Calvin goes further. He says that no one has made much progress in the school of Christ who does not joyfully look forward to the day of death and of the final resurrection (Institutes 3.9.5). This is a hard saying, and he knows it. Most of us fear death. Calvin does not despise the fear; it is natural. But he says that the believer should overcome it by setting before his eyes what lies beyond.

For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better. PHILIPPIANS 1:23

He asks: if it is a good thing to leave a ruined, decaying house for a solid and lasting one, why should we be afraid to leave the tent of this body for the building of God? Death is not the end of life but the door into it. The one who belongs to Christ goes home.

In his sermon on Enduring Persecution for Christ Calvin makes the same point as a spur to courage. The athletes of the ancient world, he says, endured every hardship for a crown of leaves, and died for a prize they were not sure of winning. God offers us an immortal crown, and He does not ask us to fight at haphazard, for we have a promise of the prize. “Our triumph is prepared,” he says, “and yet we do all we can to shun the combat.”

A double use of the present life

The chapter that follows (Institutes 3.10) completes the picture by teaching how to use this present life and its good things. Here Calvin steers between two errors. On one side are those who would allow themselves only what is strictly necessary, and treat every pleasure as a sin. Calvin thinks this makes consciences far narrower than Scripture does. On the other side are those who use the world as if there were no heaven, and sink into luxury.

His rule is simple. We should use God’s gifts for the purpose for which He gave them, and He gave them not only for our need but for our delight. We should use them with thankfulness, with moderation, with patience when they are lacking, and with the knowledge that we must give account of them. And we should use them as those who are passing through.

But this I say, brethren, the time is short: it remaineth, that both they that have wives be as though they had none … and they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away. 1 CORINTHIANS 7:29–31

Hope that steadies the heart

It is easy to caricature Calvin’s teaching here as gloomy other-worldliness. It is better read as a steadying hope. A person who knows where he is going can travel through hardship without being crushed. The refugees in Geneva who had lost homes, lands and families could hear Calvin say that this world was not their home, and find comfort, not despair. They had a better country.

But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city. HEBREWS 11:16

The honest caution is that Calvin’s strong language about contempt for the world, taken alone, could encourage a coldness towards the good things of creation and towards the needs of this world. That is not where he meant to lead, as his own labours for the poor and the refugee show. The hope of heaven, rightly held, does not make us careless of earth. It makes us free to spend ourselves on earth, because we are not trying to secure our treasure here.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Set aside ten minutes this week to think deliberately about the life to come. Read Revelation 21:1–7 slowly.

2. Name a trouble that has loosened your grip on this world. Thank God for what it has taught you.

3. Ask yourself honestly whether you fear death. Bring that fear to Christ, who has gone through death before you.

4. Consider whether you have been too strict or too careless in using God’s gifts. Ask for thankfulness and moderation.

5. Let the hope of heaven make you more generous here. Give something away this week that you would otherwise have kept.

A PRAYER
Lord, I love this world too much and think about my true home too little.
Use my troubles to loosen my grip on what is passing, and to lift my eyes to what is eternal.
Let me receive this present life with thanks, as Your gift, and hold it loosely, as a pilgrim.
Take away my fear of death, and give me a joyful longing for the day when I shall be with Christ, which is far better. Amen.

fields.title: The Main Hinge of Religion
fields.body_html:
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. ROMANS 3:24

Having spent many chapters on faith, repentance and the Christian life, Calvin turns at last in Institutes 3.11 to the doctrine at the heart of the Reformation. He introduces it with a famous phrase. Justification, he says in effect, is the main hinge on which religion turns, and so we must give it all the more attention. Unless you first grasp how you stand before God, and what His judgement is concerning you, you have no foundation on which to build your salvation, nor on which to build piety towards God.

What justification means

Calvin defines justification with legal precision, which is not surprising in a man trained as a lawyer. To be justified, he says, is to be reckoned righteous in God’s judgement and accepted because of that righteousness. And since no one is righteous in himself, justification by faith means this: that a person, excluded from the righteousness of works, grasps the righteousness of Christ through faith, and, clothed in it, appears in God’s sight not as a sinner but as a righteous man (Institutes 3.11.2).

And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. PHILIPPIANS 3:9

In short, justification consists of two things: the forgiveness of sins and the imputation of Christ’s righteousness. God does not merely wipe the slate clean and leave it blank. He writes on it the perfect obedience of His Son.

Even as David also describeth the blessedness of the man, unto whom God imputeth righteousness without works, saying, Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. ROMANS 4:6–7

A declaration, not a process

The crucial point, for Calvin as for Luther, is that justification is God’s verdict, not a gradual process of being made good. It is like a judge declaring a person acquitted, not like a doctor slowly healing a patient. Calvin knew very well that God also heals; that is sanctification, the second part of the double grace. But the two must not be confused. If our acceptance with God depended even in part on how holy we had become, no one could ever be sure of it, because our holiness is always imperfect.

Calvin puts it vividly. If you examine even the best work of the holiest person, you will find in it something of the rottenness of the flesh (Institutes 3.14.9). Before God’s perfect judgement, the finest of our deeds would be condemned. Our only hope is to be clothed in a righteousness that is not our own.

But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags. ISAIAH 64:6

This is why he says, in his sermon on All Scripture in the Ochorus library, that men may boast as much as they please that their works are virtuous and holy, but when they appear before the heavenly judge, all will be as chaff.

Faith as an empty hand

How then do we receive this righteousness? By faith alone. And Calvin is careful to say that faith does not justify because it is itself a virtue that earns God’s favour. Faith justifies only because it receives Christ. He compares faith to an earthen pot (Institutes 3.11.7). It has no value in itself; its value is the treasure it holds. Or, as others have put it after him, faith is an empty hand held out to receive a gift.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast. EPHESIANS 2:8–9

This leaves no room for pride. Everything we are given, we are given freely. Our faith itself is God’s gift.

Peace of conscience

Why did Calvin care so much about this? Not because he loved controversy, though he engaged in plenty. He cared because of the peace of troubled consciences. He had seen people tormented by the question of whether they had done enough, confessed enough, suffered enough. He believed that the only way to quiet a conscience before God is to show it Christ’s righteousness, perfect and complete, given freely.

Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. ROMANS 5:1

He saw, too, that this peace is the only true ground for glad obedience. A person who serves God in order to be accepted will serve Him anxiously, like a hired servant. A person who knows he is already accepted will serve Him freely, like a son. Calvin has a lovely passage on this in Institutes 3.19.5, on Christian freedom: God, he says, treats us like a father who receives with delight even the small, imperfect efforts of his children, because they are his children.

Faith alone, but never alone

Calvin’s opponents accused the Reformers of making good works unnecessary. Calvin answered with a sentence that has often been summarised in a Reformation saying: it is faith alone that justifies, but the faith that justifies is not alone. He puts it in his own way (Institutes 3.16.1). Christ justifies no one whom He does not also sanctify. We are justified not without works, yet not through works, since in our sharing in Christ, which justifies us, sanctification is included as much as righteousness.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. JAMES 2:17

This is why Calvin placed the chapters on the Christian life before justification. He wanted no one to think that the free forgiveness of sins made holiness optional.

A caution for the reader

Calvin’s doctrine of justification is among the clearest statements of the gospel ever written, and it deserves to be read by every Christian. But his long disputes with Rome on the subject in Institutes 3.11–18 are heavy with polemic, and they sometimes set the opposing position in its worst light. The modern reader will do well to take Calvin’s positive teaching to heart and to read his polemic with charity towards those he was answering, many of whom were also sincerely seeking to honour God’s grace.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. ROMANS 8:1
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask the question Calvin says we must answer first: how do I stand before God, and on what ground?

2. Name one way in which you have been trying to earn God’s acceptance. Lay it down and receive Christ’s righteousness as a gift.

3. Read Romans 4 slowly, and notice how Abraham and David were both justified by faith.

4. If your conscience is troubled, speak to it the words of Romans 8:1 until it believes them.

5. Consider whether your obedience has been that of a hired servant or a beloved child, and ask for a child’s freedom.

A PRAYER
Holy God, I cannot stand before You in my own righteousness; my best works are stained, and my heart is not pure.
Thank You that in Christ You forgive all my sins and clothe me in His perfect obedience.
Quiet my troubled conscience with the peace that comes from being justified by faith.
And let that peace make me holy, so that I serve You gladly, not as a hired servant but as Your child. Amen.

fields.title: The Chief Exercise of Faith
fields.body_html:
Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. MATTHEW 7:7

The longest chapter in the whole of the Institutes is not about predestination, or the sacraments, or the church. It is about prayer. Institutes 3.20 runs to more than fifty sections, and its title tells us how Calvin thought of it: prayer is the chief exercise of faith, by which we daily receive God’s benefits. For a man remembered chiefly as a systematic theologian, that is worth noticing. His theology was meant to end on its knees.

Digging up the treasure

Calvin begins by drawing together everything he has said so far. We have learned that we are empty and destitute of every good, and that all our help is in God, who has offered it to us freely in Christ. Calvin raises the obvious objection himself. If God already knows what we need, and has decreed what He will do, why should we pray? This is a beautiful answer, and it removes the fear that prayer is pointless. God does not need informing. We need forming. Prayer is the school in which faith is trained.

Four rules for prayer

Calvin gives four rules for right prayer (Institutes 3.20.4–14), and they are worth learning by heart.

The first is reverence. We must come to God with minds set free from earthly cares, as those who are speaking to the King of heaven. Calvin warns against prayer that is careless, distracted or irreverent, as if we were talking to an equal.

The second is a sincere sense of need, joined with repentance. We must truly feel our lack and truly want what we ask. Many prayers, Calvin says, are recited as a mere duty, with no real desire behind them. He also insists that we must not come to God while clinging to sins we mean to keep.

The third is humility, which gives up all confidence in ourselves. We must come not trusting our own worthiness but pleading only God’s mercy. The saints of Scripture, even the holiest, came as beggars.

The fourth is confident hope. Humble as we are, we must pray in the firm expectation that we will be heard. Behind all four rules stands the Mediator. Calvin insists that we can come to God only in the name of Christ. He speaks sharply against praying to the saints, which he believed took from Christ the honour that is His alone (Institutes 3.20.21–27). In his sermon on All Scripture Calvin makes the connection clear: our confidence to call upon God comes from knowing that He will not cast us off when we come in the name of Him who is appointed our advocate.

He also says that the first three petitions are given to God’s glory, and the last three to our needs, and that we must learn to seek His glory first.

Finally, Calvin urges both persistence and order. We must not give up if God seems slow to answer; sometimes He delays to exercise our faith. Calvin’s rules can sound daunting, as if no prayer could ever meet them. He anticipates this. God, he says, does not reject prayers because of their weakness, if they are sincere; He pardons the faults in them. No one has ever prayed perfectly. The rules are a guide, not a barrier. 4. Pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly, one petition a day, letting each one shape what you ask for.

Hallowed be Your name, Your kingdom come, Your will be done. Hear me, and make me persevere. Amen.

fields.title: The Dreadful Decree
fields.body_html:
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love. EPHESIANS 1:4

It is impossible to write honestly about Calvin without writing about predestination, and impossible to write about it without care. It is the doctrine most often associated with his name, and the one most often misunderstood — by admirers and critics alike. The first thing to notice is where Calvin placed it. In the final edition of the Institutes he did not put it at the beginning, with the doctrine of God, as if it were the foundation of everything. He put it near the end of the third book (3.21–24), after faith, repentance, justification and prayer. He treated it as a truth for believers, to be pondered by those who already know themselves saved by grace, not as a riddle to be solved before coming to Christ.

Neither curiosity nor silence

Calvin opens with a double warning (Institutes 3.21.1–4). On the one hand, human curiosity makes this subject dangerous. If we try to break into the secret places of God’s wisdom, he says, we will enter a labyrinth from which there is no way out. We must go as far as Scripture leads and stop where it stops. On the other hand, we must not be so afraid of the subject that we refuse to speak of it at all, for God has revealed it in His Word for our good. The rule, he says, is to be neither more curious nor more silent than Scripture.

The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever. DEUTERONOMY 29:29

He preached the same caution in his sermon God Will Have All Men to Be Saved, in the Ochorus library: “We must not strive to know any more of God’s counsel, than what is revealed in holy writ.”

What Calvin taught

Calvin defines predestination as God’s eternal decree, by which He determined with Himself what He willed to become of each person (Institutes 3.21.5). Some are foreordained to eternal life, others to eternal condemnation. He believed Scripture taught both sides of this: that God freely chooses some in Christ, from no merit of their own, and that He passes by others, leaving them to the just consequences of their sin. This second part is usually called reprobation.

For the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth. ROMANS 9:11

He did not pretend this was easy. In Institutes 3.23.7 he says of the decree that it is dreadful, and he admits it. His Latin word can also mean awe-inspiring, but either way he was confessing that it made him tremble. He insisted that God acts justly, even where we cannot see how, and that those who are condemned are condemned for their own sin, which they cannot blame on God. And he warned repeatedly against asking why God chooses one and not another. In the sermon he says plainly: “we know not why this man was chosen in preference to that,” and still we must confess that whatever God does is just.

The purpose of election

What Calvin cared about most was the use of the doctrine, and here he is warm and pastoral. Election, he says, has three great fruits for believers.

First, humility. If God chose us before we were born, before we had done good or evil, then we have nothing to boast of. In the sermon he says that election “serveth to humble us, knowing that our salvation hangeth not upon our deserts.” We are no better than others; we all come from the cursed root of Adam.

For who maketh thee to differ from another? and what hast thou that thou didst not receive? 1 CORINTHIANS 4:7

Second, assurance. Calvin believed that the believer can rest in God’s choice, because it does not depend on his own weak hold on God but on God’s unchanging hold on him. “We are as birds upon the boughs,” he says in the same sermon, “and set forth as a prey to satan.” What assurance could we have of tomorrow unless God, who called us, will finish the work He began?

My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me: And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand. JOHN 10:27–28

Third, gratitude and praise. Election is a doctrine that ends in worship, as Paul’s great argument in Romans 9–11 ends in doxology.

Christ the mirror of election

The most important pastoral counsel Calvin gives is this: we must never try to discover our election by looking into God’s secret decree. That way lies madness. We must look to Christ. He calls Christ the mirror in which we must, and without self-deception may, contemplate our own election (Institutes 3.24.5). If we are in communion with Christ, we have a sure testimony that we are written in the book of life. The question is never, am I elect? The question is, do I trust Christ? And if I do, I may be sure.

All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. JOHN 6:37

Honest cautions

Having said all that, the reader must be told plainly where Calvin should be read with care.

First, his teaching on reprobation — that God actively ordains some to condemnation — has troubled many who love his teaching on grace. Scripture certainly teaches God’s sovereign choice. It also teaches, with great force, His sincere love for the world, His pleasure in the repentance of sinners, and His free offer of Christ to all. Calvin believed these could be held together, and he speaks of God’s will in two ways, His secret counsel and His revealed will. But many faithful Christians, including many in his own tradition, have found that his system at times lets the hidden decree overshadow the open invitation.

Second, his reading of certain texts is open to question. In the sermon on 1 Timothy 2:4 he insists that God will have all men to be saved means all sorts and conditions of men, not every individual. That is a possible reading, but not the only one, and the reader should weigh it against the whole of Scripture.

Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord GOD: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? EZEKIEL 18:23

Third, it should be said in his favour that the very same sermon is full of urgency for the lost. Because God will have people of every nation saved, Calvin says, we must labour to bring those who are far off and pray for them. “Jesus Christ is not only a Saviour of few,” he says, “but he offereth himself to all.” Calvin’s doctrine of election did not make him careless of missions; Geneva sent preachers into France at the risk of their lives.

The wise reader will hold the doctrine as Calvin at his best held it: with trembling, with humility, and with eyes fixed on Christ.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If this doctrine troubles you, do not try to look into God’s secret counsel. Look to Christ, and ask whether you trust Him.

2. Read Romans 8:28–39 and notice how Paul uses God’s purpose to give comfort, not to raise fear.

3. Let election humble you. Name one way you have thought yourself better than others, and confess it.

4. Pray this week for someone who seems far from God, remembering that Christ offers Himself to all.

5. Where you cannot reconcile what Scripture teaches, write down the texts on both sides and hold them together before God.

A PRAYER
Sovereign Lord, Your ways are higher than mine, and Your judgements are past finding out.
Keep me from prying into what You have hidden, and from being silent about what You have revealed.
Let me find my assurance not in my own grip on You but in Christ, who will never cast out any who come.
Make me humble, thankful and urgent for the salvation of others, and let all my thoughts of You end in worship. Amen.

fields.title: The Mother of Believers
fields.body_html:
Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen. EPHESIANS 3:21

The fourth and final book of the Institutes concerns what Calvin calls the external means or aids by which God invites us into the society of Christ and keeps us there. It begins with the church. And here Calvin, often thought of as a stern individualist, speaks with remarkable tenderness. He borrows an image from the early church father Cyprian: the church is our mother (Institutes 4.1.1–4).

A mother to her children

God could perfect His people in a moment, Calvin says, but He has chosen to bring them to maturity through the church’s care. There is no other way into life, he writes, unless this mother conceive us in her womb, give us birth, nourish us at her breast, and keep us under her care and guidance until we put off mortal flesh and become like the angels. Away from her bosom, he adds, one cannot hope for any forgiveness of sins or any salvation (Institutes 4.1.4).

And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ. EPHESIANS 4:11–12

This is a strong statement from a man who had broken with Rome. But Calvin did not believe he had left the church. He believed he was reforming it. And he was sure that no Christian could grow alone. We are weak, and God, in His kindness, gives us the preaching of the Word, the sacraments and the fellowship of believers to nourish us, as a mother nourishes a child.

Visible and invisible

Calvin distinguishes, as Augustine did, between the church as God sees it and the church as we see it (Institutes 4.1.7). The invisible church is all the elect of every age, known only to God. The visible church is the company of those on earth who profess to worship one God in Christ, are baptised, share the Lord’s Supper and hear the Word. In the visible church, Calvin admits, many hypocrites are mixed with the true. But we must honour it and keep communion with it, because it is where God has promised to meet us.

Let both grow together until the harvest. MATTHEW 13:30

The marks of the church

How can we recognise a true church? Calvin gives a short answer that became standard in Reformed teaching. Wherever we see the Word of God purely preached and heard, and the sacraments administered according to Christ’s institution, there, it is not to be doubted, a church of God exists (Institutes 4.1.9).

Then they that gladly received his word were baptized … And they continued stedfastly in the apostles’ doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers. ACTS 2:41–42

The strength of this answer is its simplicity. A true church is not one that is free of sin, or one with an unbroken line of bishops, or one that is large and splendid. It is one where Christ speaks through His Word and gives Himself in His sacraments.

And Calvin draws a humble consequence. Where these marks are present, he says, we must not leave a church lightly because of the faults of its members, or even because of lesser errors in doctrine (Institutes 4.1.12–16). He was scathing about people who separate from every church in search of a perfectly pure one. No such church exists on earth. The Christian who is impatient of imperfection should look first at himself.

In his sermon on All Scripture Calvin shows what he thought the heart of a true pulpit was: “When we go into the pulpit, we ought to be assured that it is God that sent us, and that we bring the message which he committed to us.”

Four offices

Calvin believed that Scripture gave the church a pattern for its ministry. fields.body_html:
The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 CORINTHIANS 10:16

The Reformation divided Christians over many things, but over none more painfully than the Lord’s Supper. Rome, Luther, Zwingli and the Anabaptists all held different views, and the Protestants themselves could not agree. Calvin spent much of his life trying to find a way through, and his teaching on the sacraments, set out in Institutes 4.14–18 and in his Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper of 1541, is among the most thoughtful and devotional things he wrote.

Why God gives signs

Calvin begins with our weakness. We are creatures of flesh, he says, and our faith is so feeble that unless it is propped up on every side it wavers and falls. So God, in His kindness, accommodates Himself to our capacity. Since we are earthly, He leads us to Himself by earthly elements, and sets before us in the flesh a mirror of spiritual blessings (Institutes 4.14.3).

He defines a sacrament as an outward sign by which the Lord seals on our consciences the promises of His goodwill towards us, to support the weakness of our faith; and by which we in turn testify our devotion to Him before Him, the angels and the world (Institutes 4.14.1). Following Augustine, he calls a sacrament a visible word. It does not add anything to the promise of the gospel. It shows the same promise in a form we can see, touch and taste.

And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith which he had yet being uncircumcised. ROMANS 4:11

This means that sacraments are never separated from the Word. A sign without a promise is empty. Calvin was sharp with the medieval practice of saying the words of the sacrament in Latin that the people could not understand, as if they worked like a spell. The Word must be preached, he said, so that the sign can be understood and received by faith.

Baptism

Calvin taught that baptism is the sign of our initiation into the church, by which we are engrafted into Christ and reckoned among God’s children. It signifies the washing away of our sins and our death and new life in Christ. He defended the baptism of the infant children of believers at length (Institutes 4.16), chiefly on the ground that God’s covenant promise includes the children of His people, as circumcision did in the Old Testament. Christians of the Baptist tradition, many of whom share Calvin’s doctrine of grace, have not been persuaded, and the reader may weigh the arguments on both sides.

For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call. ACTS 2:39

The Supper: truly fed

It is on the Lord’s Supper that Calvin is most distinctive. He rejected the Roman doctrine of transubstantiation, which taught that the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ in substance. He also rejected Luther’s teaching that Christ’s body is present everywhere and so present in, with and under the bread. Christ’s human body, Calvin believed, is truly human, and so is in one place — at the right hand of the Father in heaven.

But he was just as firm that the Supper is not merely a memorial, a reminder of something absent. In the Supper, he insisted, believers truly receive Christ, His body and blood, and are truly fed by Him. The sign is not empty. What it signifies is truly given.

I am the living bread which came down from heaven: if any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever: and the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. JOHN 6:51

How can both be true? Calvin’s answer is the Holy Spirit. The Spirit truly unites things separated in space. By the secret power of the Spirit, we are lifted up to heaven to feed on Christ, and His life is poured into us (Institutes 4.17.10, 18, 31). This is why the old liturgies said, Lift up your hearts. Calvin admits that this is a mystery too high for his mind to grasp or his words to express, and he says frankly that he would rather experience it than understand it (Institutes 4.17.32).

This is the same teaching of union with Christ that runs through all his work. The Supper does not give a different Christ from the one we receive by faith in the Word. It gives the same Christ, in a way fitted to our weakness. In his sermon The Mystery of Godliness Calvin speaks of Christ joining Himself to us so that we are made partakers of His substance; in the Supper, he believed, that union is sealed and nourished.

Whoso eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, hath eternal life; and I will raise him up at the last day. JOHN 6:54

Coming to the table

Calvin wanted the Supper to be celebrated often. He believed it should be given at least every week, and argued for it in the Institutes (4.17.43–46). The magistrates of Geneva would allow it only four times a year, and he had to accept that, though he recorded his disagreement. It is a striking fact that the man often blamed for coldness in worship wanted his people at the table more often than most Protestants have been since.

He also wrote tenderly about who should come. The Supper, he said, is not for the perfect but for the weak. Those who are troubled by their sins and hungry for grace are exactly the ones for whom it was given. It is medicine for the sick, not a reward for the healthy. Worthiness means not sinlessness but faith and repentance.

Let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:28

Polemic and peace

Calvin laboured for agreement among the Protestants. In 1549 he and Heinrich Bullinger of Zurich reached a common statement on the sacraments, the Zurich Consensus, which drew the Swiss churches together. But the same agreement provoked a Lutheran pastor, Joachim Westphal, to attack it, and Calvin answered him in a series of increasingly bitter treatises. It is sad to see a doctrine of communion become the occasion of such anger. The modern reader may be grateful for Calvin’s teaching and grieved by his tone, and learn from both.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before you next come to the Lord’s Table, read John 6:47–58 and ask the Spirit to lift your heart to Christ.

2. Remember your baptism. Thank God for the promise it signified, and ask how you are living out your death and new life in Christ.

3. If you have stayed away from communion because you feel unworthy, remember that it is medicine for the weak.

4. Ask whether you value the sacraments as God’s gifts to your faith, or treat them as optional extras.

5. Pray for Christians with whom you disagree about the sacraments, and resolve to speak of them charitably.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You know how weak my faith is, and You have given me signs I can see and touch and taste.
In the bread and the cup, feed me with Yourself. Lift my heart by Your Spirit to where You are.
Seal to me the promise of Your love, and nourish the union You have made between us.
Forgive Your church for her quarrels at Your table, and draw us together in the communion of Your body and blood. Amen.

fields.title: The Two Governments
fields.body_html:
Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. MATTHEW 22:21

The Institutes ends not with heaven, or with the church, but with the state. Its last chapter (4.20) is on civil government. That may seem an odd place to finish a book about the knowledge of God, but Calvin had reasons. He was writing in a century when Christians were being burned by kings, when some radicals taught that believers should have nothing to do with government, and when others wanted to overthrow all rulers in the name of Christ. He believed that the Christian needed to know how to live under earthly authority, and he gave the question careful thought.

A twofold government

Calvin begins by distinguishing two kinds of government in human life (Institutes 3.19.15; 4.20.1). One is spiritual, by which the conscience is instructed in godliness and the worship of God. The other is political, by which a person is taught the duties of humanity and citizenship that must be kept among men. The first concerns the inner life of the soul and eternal life. The second concerns outward behaviour and the life of this world. They are different, and must not be confused. But they are not opposed.

Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. ROMANS 13:1

Against those who said that Christians should keep clear of government altogether, Calvin argued that civil authority is a gift of God. Its purpose, as long as we live among men, is to protect outward worship, to defend sound doctrine and the standing of the church, to shape our conduct to the requirements of human society, to promote peace and justice, and to keep common order (Institutes 4.20.2). Without it, he said, human life would be worse than that of beasts. It is as necessary as bread, water, sun and air, and far more excellent.

A holy calling

Calvin’s most striking claim is that the office of magistrate is a calling from God, and not only a lawful one but, he says, the most sacred and by far the most honourable of all callings in the whole life of mortal men (Institutes 4.20.4). He points to the judges and kings of Israel, and to Scripture’s description of rulers as God’s ministers.

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. ROMANS 13:4

This raised the standard for rulers as much as it raised their dignity. If they are God’s ministers, they must answer to Him. They must protect the poor, the widow and the orphan, do justice without partiality, and remember that they will give account. Calvin was no flatterer of princes. His commentaries and sermons are full of warnings to rulers who forget God.

He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. 2 SAMUEL 23:3

Obedience and its limits

Calvin taught that Christians must obey their rulers, and not only good ones. Even an unjust ruler, he said, holds his authority from God, and private persons are not to take up arms against him. We should pray for rulers, pay our taxes, obey the laws and bear injustice patiently, remembering that God can judge wicked kings in His own time.

But he placed two important limits on this obedience. The first is that in some constitutions there are lesser magistrates — he mentions the ephors of Sparta and the estates of a realm — whose office it is to restrain the tyranny of kings. If they fail to do so, he says, they betray the liberty of the people, of which they are the appointed guardians (Institutes 4.20.31). This short passage had a long history. Later Reformed thinkers developed it into a doctrine of resistance to tyranny, and it played a part in the growth of constitutional government.

The second limit is absolute. In obedience to rulers we must always make one exception: that it must never lead us away from obedience to God. If rulers command anything against Him, it must count for nothing. The final words of the Institutes quote the apostles.

Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. ACTS 5:29

Calvin adds that we were bought at a great price by Christ, so that we should not become slaves to the wicked desires of men, still less to their ungodliness. His own life bears it out. He wrote the Institutes as a defence of believers whom the king of France was persecuting.

The shadow of Servetus

And here, honestly, we must turn back to the darkest page of Calvin’s story. Among the tasks Calvin assigned to civil government was the protection of true religion and the punishment of public blasphemy. It was on that principle that Geneva tried and burned Michael Servetus in 1553, with Calvin as his accuser. Calvin himself refers to it from the pulpit in The Mystery of Godliness, in the Ochorus library, speaking of Servetus as a detestable heretic “who was here put to death.”

And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. 2 TIMOTHY 2:24–25

It is true that almost every government of the time, Catholic and Protestant, punished heresy with death, and that the Swiss churches endorsed the verdict. It is true that Calvin asked for a less cruel form of execution. But it is also true that some of his contemporaries saw more clearly. The humanist Sebastian Castellio, who had once worked with Calvin in Geneva, wrote against the execution; his protest is remembered for the principle that to kill a man is not to defend a doctrine but simply to kill a man. Calvin replied with a defence of the punishment of heretics. On this, Calvin was wrong and his critic was right.

The lesson for Christians is not that Calvin’s teaching on government is worthless; much of it is wise. It is that the confusion he warned against, between the spiritual and the civil government, was in this case the very confusion he fell into. The sword of the magistrate cannot defend the truth of the Trinity. Only the Word and Spirit can do that.

For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds. 2 CORINTHIANS 10:4
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Pray this week by name for those who govern your country, your region and your town.

2. Consider whether you honour the calling of public service, or treat all politics with contempt.

3. Ask whether there is any point at which obedience to a law or ruler would lead you away from God. Settle your answer now.

4. Reflect on the death of Servetus. Ask where Christians today are still tempted to use power to enforce belief.

5. If you hold public office or influence of any kind, ask how you are serving as God’s minister for the good of others.

A PRAYER
King of kings, all authority on earth is from You, and all rulers must give account to You.
Give wisdom, justice and mercy to those who govern us, and make us quiet, prayerful and honest citizens.
Where rulers command what You forbid, give us courage to obey You rather than men.
Forgive the church for every time she has used the sword to defend Your truth, and teach us to trust Your Word and Spirit alone. Amen.

The other is political, by which a person is taught the duties of humanity and citizenship that must be kept among men. The first concerns the inner life of the soul and eternal life. The second concerns outward behaviour and the life of this world. They are different, and must not be confused. But they are not opposed. Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. ROMANS 13:1 Against those who said that Christians should keep clear of government altogether, Calvin argued that civil authority is a gift of God. Its purpose, as long as we live among men, is to protect outward worship, to defend sound doctrine and the standing of the church, to shape our conduct to the requirements of human society, to promote peace and justice, and to keep common order (Institutes 4.20.2). Without it, he said, human life would be worse than that of beasts. It is as necessary as bread, water, sun and air, and far more excellent. A holy calling Calvin’s most striking claim is that the office of magistrate is a calling from God, and not only a lawful one but, he says, the most sacred and by far the most honourable of all callings in the whole life of mortal men (Institutes 4.20.4). He points to the judges and kings of Israel, and to Scripture’s description of rulers as God’s ministers. For he is the minister of God to thee for good. He that ruleth over men must be just, ruling in the fear of God. 2 SAMUEL 23:3 Obedience and its limits Calvin taught that Christians must obey their rulers, and not only good ones. If they fail to do so, he says, they betray the liberty of the people, of which they are the appointed guardians (Institutes 4.20.31). This short passage had a long history. Later Reformed thinkers developed it into a doctrine of resistance to tyranny, and it played a part in the growth of constitutional government. The second limit is absolute. In obedience to rulers we must always make one exception: that it must never lead us away from obedience to God. If rulers command anything against Him, it must count for nothing. The final words of the Institutes quote the apostles. Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. He wrote the Institutes as a defence of believers whom the king of France was persecuting. The shadow of Servetus And here, honestly, we must turn back to the darkest page of Calvin’s story. Among the tasks Calvin assigned to civil government was the protection of true religion and the punishment of public blasphemy. It was on that principle that Geneva tried and burned Michael Servetus in 1553, with Calvin as his accuser. Calvin himself refers to it from the pulpit in The Mystery of Godliness, in the Ochorus library, speaking of Servetus as a detestable heretic “who was here put to death.” And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. 2 TIMOTHY 2:24–25 It is true that almost every government of the time, Catholic and Protestant, punished heresy with death, and that the Swiss churches endorsed the verdict. It is true that Calvin asked for a less cruel form of execution. But it is also true that some of his contemporaries saw more clearly. The humanist Sebastian Castellio, who had once worked with Calvin in Geneva, wrote against the execution; his protest is remembered for the principle that to kill a man is not to defend a doctrine but simply to kill a man. Calvin replied with a defence of the punishment of heretics. On this, Calvin was wrong and his critic was right. The lesson for Christians is not that Calvin’s teaching on government is worthless; much of it is wise. It is that the confusion he warned against, between the spiritual and the civil government, was in this case the very confusion he fell into. The sword of the magistrate cannot defend the truth of the Trinity. Only the Word and Spirit can do that. For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds. 2 CORINTHIANS 10:4 FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Pray this week by name for those who govern your country, your region and your town. 2. Consider whether you honour the calling of public service, or treat all politics with contempt. 3. Ask whether there is any point at which obedience to a law or ruler would lead you away from God. Settle your answer now. 4. Reflect on the death of Servetus. Ask where Christians today are still tempted to use power to enforce belief. 5. If you hold public office or influence of any kind, ask how you are serving as God’s minister for the good of others. A PRAYER King of kings, all authority on earth is from You, and all rulers must give account to You. Give wisdom, justice and mercy to those who govern us, and make us quiet, prayerful and honest citizens. Where rulers command what You forbid, give us courage to obey You rather than men. Forgive the church for every time she has used the sword to defend Your truth, and teach us to trust Your Word and Spirit alone. Amen.

fields.title: Every Calling a Post
fields.body_html:
Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called. 1 CORINTHIANS 7:20

Among the many ways Calvin changed the way Christians think, few have reached so deep into ordinary life as his teaching on calling. In the medieval church a vocation usually meant a call to the priesthood or the monastery. The truly religious life was lived apart from the world, and ordinary work — farming, trade, housekeeping, craft — was a lower way. The Reformers overturned that. Luther taught that the milkmaid and the cobbler serve God as truly as the monk. Calvin took up the same conviction and gave it a memorable form.

A sentry post

At the end of his chapters on the Christian life, Calvin writes that the Lord bids each one of us, in all life’s actions, to look to his calling (Institutes 3.10.6). He knows how restless the human heart is, how ambition drives us to grasp at many things at once, how easily we are carried hither and thither. So, to keep us from confusion, He has appointed duties for every person in his particular way of life. And He has named these various kinds of living callings, so that no one may thoughtlessly wander about. Each person’s way of life, Calvin says, is a sort of sentry post assigned to him by the Lord.

But as God hath distributed to every man, as the Lord hath called every one, so let him walk. 1 CORINTHIANS 7:17

The image is military, and it fits Calvin’s view of the Christian life as service. A sentry does not choose his post, and he does not leave it because it is dull or cold. He stays where he has been placed, because his commander placed him there, and because the whole army depends on each man holding his ground.

No task too humble

The comfort in this teaching is great. Calvin draws it out at once. From this, he says, a singular consolation follows: no task will be so sordid and base, provided you obey your calling in it, that it will not shine and be reckoned very precious in God’s sight.

And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. COLOSSIANS 3:23

This transformed the dignity of work. The woman at the washtub and the man at the plough are doing holy work if they do it as God’s servants. There is no secular and sacred division in Calvin’s world. There is only faithful and unfaithful service. The whole of life is lived before God.

It also transformed its burdens. Calvin notes that the person who knows he is in his calling will bear its hardships, troubles, weariness and anxieties more easily, because he knows God has laid them on him. A magistrate will discharge his office more willingly, the father of a family will do his duty more faithfully, and each will bear the inconveniences of his lot without complaint.

Diligence and generosity

Calvin’s city was busy with trade and craft, and the refugees who poured into it brought skills with them — printing, watchmaking, silk-weaving. Calvin encouraged diligence and honest work. He had a realistic view of commerce, and he was willing to allow the lending of money at moderate interest, which the medieval church had forbidden, while he insisted that it must never oppress the poor and must be governed by the law of love.

Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men. PROVERBS 22:29

But he was equally clear that the purpose of work is not the accumulation of wealth for ourselves. It is the service of God and our neighbour. We saw in an earlier chapter that Calvin taught every gift is held in stewardship. Work is one of the chief ways we serve others; its fruits are to be shared. The prosperous are to relieve the needy.

Let him that stole steal no more: but rather let him labour, working with his hands the thing which is good, that he may have to give to him that needeth. EPHESIANS 4:28

Contentment and change

Does this mean no one should ever change their work or station? Calvin did not think so. He himself had changed from law to the ministry. The point is not that we can never move, but that we must not wander about restlessly, driven by ambition or discontent. If God opens a door, we may go through it. But we are to be content where we are placed until He does, and faithful in whatever post He has given us.

Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. PHILIPPIANS 4:11

An honest word

Calvin’s teaching on calling has been enormously influential, and not all its later uses would have pleased him. In the twentieth century the sociologist Max Weber famously linked what he called the Protestant ethic to the rise of capitalism. Historians still argue about how far he was right. Whatever the truth, Calvin himself cannot be made the prophet of acquisition. He warned constantly against greed, luxury and the oppression of the poor.

It is also fair to say that in Calvin’s world, a person’s calling was often closely tied to the social station into which he was born, and his counsel to stay at one’s post could be heard as a reason to accept injustice. The modern reader may take his central insight — that all honest work is holy when done for God — without concluding that every station in life is fixed by heaven.

Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 10:31
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name your present post: your work, your family responsibilities, your place in the church. Thank God for placing you there.

2. Think of the dullest or lowliest task you must do this week. Do it deliberately as service to God.

3. Ask whether restlessness or ambition has been making you wander in heart from where God has placed you.

4. Consider how the fruits of your work could serve others more generously, and act on one idea.

5. If you are considering a change of work, pray for wisdom to know whether it is God’s leading or your own discontent.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have set me at my post, and You have not placed me there by accident.
Keep me from restlessness and envy, and make me faithful in the work You have given me.
Let me do even the humblest task as unto You, so that it may shine in Your sight.
Use my work to serve my neighbour and to glorify Your name, and make me generous with all it brings. Amen.

fields.title: Songs God Put in Our Mouths
fields.body_html:
O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation. PSALM 95:1

People who think of Calvin as a man without joy should spend an evening with the Genevan Psalter. It is one of the great treasures of Christian worship, and Calvin laboured over it for more than twenty years. The tune many English-speaking Christians know as the Old Hundredth, sung to All people that on earth do dwell, first appeared in a Genevan edition of the Psalms. Wherever Calvin’s teaching went — to France, the Netherlands, Hungary, Scotland — congregations went singing the Psalms.

Giving the people back their song

In the medieval church the people rarely sang. The choir and the clergy sang in Latin; the congregation watched and listened. The Reformers wanted to give the whole people of God their voice. Luther did it with hymns. Calvin did it with the Psalms.

His very first attempt came early. In the Articles he and Farel drew up for Geneva in 1537 they asked that psalms be sung in church. During his exile in Strasbourg, where he heard German congregations singing, he gathered a small book of metrical psalms in French for his refugee congregation in 1539, including a few of his own versions. Back in Geneva he worked with the poet Clément Marot, and after Marot’s death with Theodore Beza, until the complete Psalter, all one hundred and fifty psalms set to singable tunes, was finished in 1562. Musicians, of whom Louis Bourgeois is the best known, wrote melodies of great dignity and strength.

Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord. EPHESIANS 5:19

Why the Psalms

In his preface to the Genevan form of prayers and psalms, Calvin explains why he chose the Psalms above all. Singing, he says, has great power to move and inflame the heart to call upon God and praise Him with more zeal. But because it has such power, it must be used rightly. We should sing songs that are not merely decent but holy. And where shall we find such songs? Nowhere better than in the Psalms, which the Holy Spirit Himself made. When we sing them, he says in substance, we can be certain that God puts the words in our mouths, as if He Himself sang in us to exalt His glory.

I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever: with my mouth will I make known thy faithfulness to all generations. PSALM 89:1

He also asked that church singing have weight and majesty, fitting for the presence of God and His angels, not light or frivolous. And he wanted the Psalms sung not only in church but at home and at work, so that ordinary life would be filled with praise. He hoped they would replace the careless songs of the street.

An anatomy of the soul

Calvin loved the Psalms as a teacher as well as a worshipper. In the preface to his commentary on the Psalms, the same preface in which he speaks of his sudden conversion, he calls the book an anatomy of all the parts of the soul. There is no emotion anyone can feel, he says in effect, that is not represented there as in a mirror. The Holy Spirit has drawn out all the griefs, sorrows, fears, doubts, hopes, cares, perplexities and stormy passions by which our minds are commonly troubled.

Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD. Lord, hear my voice: let thine ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications. PSALM 130:1–2

This is why the Psalms are such a gift. They give us words for every condition of the heart, and they teach us to bring every condition to God. The lament is not less holy than the song of praise. The one who prays the Psalms learns that nothing needs to be hidden from God, and that every feeling can be turned into prayer.

He saw himself in them, too. In the same preface he compares his own trials to David’s, and says that David’s experience helped him understand his own. The man who rarely spoke about himself found his inner life written out in the Psalter.

Singing with understanding

For Calvin, the heart of all this was that worship must be understood. He was insistent that prayers and songs be in the language of the people. A songbird or a parrot may sing well, he says in the same preface, but it does not understand what it sings; it is the proper gift of human beings to know what they are singing. God is honoured when His people sing with the mind as well as the voice.

I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also. 1 CORINTHIANS 14:15

A word of balance

Calvin’s concern for the purity of worship led Geneva to sing the Psalms without instruments and, for the most part, to set aside other songs. Many in the Reformed tradition kept to psalm-singing alone for centuries. Others, including Isaac Watts and many who share Calvin’s theology, came to believe that the church may also sing hymns that speak openly of Christ, since the New Testament itself is full of songs to Him. The reader may honour Calvin’s love of the Psalms without concluding that nothing else may be sung.

What should not be lost is his conviction that the Psalms belong at the centre of Christian song and prayer. Churches that have let them fall silent have lost the widest, deepest and most honest school of prayer God has given.

Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD. PSALM 150:6
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Find a metrical psalm, perhaps the Old Hundredth, and sing or say it aloud this week.

2. Name the feeling that is strongest in you today. Find a psalm that expresses it, and pray it back to God.

3. Read Psalm 130 slowly as a prayer, whether or not your circumstances match it, and let it teach you.

4. Consider whether the songs you sing in worship are rich in Scripture. Ask how you might bring more of the Psalms into them.

5. Sing something to God at home or at work, not only in church.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have put songs in our mouths, and given us in the Psalms words for every condition of the heart.
Teach me to sing with understanding, and to bring my griefs and fears as well as my joys to You.
Fill my home and my work with praise, and let my whole life become a song to Your glory.
Let everything that has breath praise You, and let me be among them. Amen.

fields.title: A School of Christ
fields.body_html:
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in. MATTHEW 25:35

Calvin’s teaching was never meant to stay in books. He was a pastor in a real city, with real poor, real sick, real refugees and real children to be taught, and he believed that the gospel must take shape in the common life of the church. The Scottish reformer John Knox, who spent time in Geneva as a refugee himself, famously called it the most perfect school of Christ since the days of the apostles. That was a generous judgement, and Geneva had its faults, as earlier chapters have shown. But three parts of its life deserve to be remembered: its care for the poor, its welcome to the stranger, and its passion for teaching.

Deacons for the poor

In his Ecclesiastical Ordinances of 1541 Calvin set the deacons among the four permanent offices of the church. He believed, from his reading of Acts 6 and the early church, that caring for the poor was not an optional charity but a ministry Christ had built into His church. In Institutes 4.3.9 he describes two kinds of deacons in the New Testament: those who administer the church’s goods for the poor, and those who give themselves to the direct care of the sick and needy.

Wherefore, brethren, look ye out among you seven men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business. ACTS 6:3

In Geneva these deacons oversaw the city’s general hospital, which cared for the sick, the old, orphans and the destitute, and they distributed relief to the poor in their homes. Calvin believed that the goods of the church belonged, above all, to the poor.
