fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. ROMANS 11:36

Twenty-one chapters may give the impression that Calvin taught a great many things, and he did. The Institutes covers almost every question a Christian might ask. But at its centre is the sentence with which it begins. True wisdom consists of two things: the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves. Everything else is that sentence followed out, patiently, carefully and reverently, through the whole of Scripture.

Follow the thread and the shape appears. God is the fountain of all good, and the world is the theatre of His glory. But our eyes are dim, and our hearts are factories of idols, so He gives us the spectacles of Scripture and seals its truth in our hearts by His Spirit. He governs all things by a Father’s hand, so that we need not fear. We were made in His image and have ruined ourselves; our wills are bound, and the law shows us our sin and stops our mouths. So God gives us a Mediator, His own Son, true God and true man, our prophet, priest and king, who bore the curse that was ours. By His Spirit He unites us to Christ, so that all Christ has becomes ours: righteousness before God and holiness of life, the double grace. We receive Him by faith, a firm and certain knowledge of God’s kindness towards us in Christ. We live a life of daily repentance, denying ourselves because we are not our own, bearing the cross, longing for the life to come, and enjoying this life’s gifts with thanks. We stand before God justified freely, clothed in a righteousness not our own. We pray, digging up the treasures laid up for us. We rest in God’s choice, looking to Christ as its mirror. And we are nourished by the church, our mother, fed by Word and sacrament, living in the world as citizens, workers at our posts, singers of the Psalms, and servants of the poor and the stranger.

What he got wrong

This book has not hidden Calvin’s faults, and it would be no tribute to him to pretend he had none.

He took part in the burning of Michael Servetus, sought the sentence and defended it afterwards. The age was cruel, but others in his own time saw that it was wrong, and he did not.

He helped build in Geneva a system of discipline that reached into private life and was enforced by civil power. Its aims were often pastoral; its methods were often harsh.

He taught a doctrine of reprobation that many faithful readers of Scripture cannot follow, and at times he read texts about God’s love for all in ways that narrowed them.

And he wrote against his opponents — Catholic, Lutheran, Anabaptist — with a contempt that his own teaching on the image of God in every person should have restrained.

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. PSALM 139:23–24

None of this is said to diminish him. It is said because he taught us to expect it. No one wrote more searchingly about the deceitfulness of the human heart, or insisted more firmly that even the best works of the holiest person are stained. He would not have wanted to be exempted from his own teaching. The proper response to his faults is not to throw him away, but to read him as he taught us to read everything: under Scripture, holding fast what is good.

What to carry away

If you carry nothing else from this book, carry three things.

First, look at God. Calvin’s whole life was an effort to get people to lift their eyes from themselves to the glory, holiness and goodness of God. Most of our troubles, he believed, come from looking too long at ourselves and too little at Him. Start each day by looking up.

I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD, which made heaven and earth. PSALM 121:1–2

Second, rest in Christ. Everything God gives, He gives in His Son. You do not have to find your righteousness in yourself, or your assurance in the secret decrees of God, or your strength in your own will. You will find all of them in Christ, and in Christ alone. Calvin’s sermons return to this again and again: we may come to Him as our brother, and worship Him as our God.

Third, give your heart. Calvin’s motto was the image of a hand holding out a heart to God, promptly and sincerely. It was not a pious slogan; it cost him everything he had wanted for himself. It is still the right response to everything this book has described. We are not our own. We belong to God. Let us live for Him.

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

A last word about the man

Calvin died on 27 May 1564, worn out by illness and work, at not quite fifty-five. He had asked to be buried without a monument, and his grave was left unmarked. He did not want a shrine. He wanted people to read the Bible, to know God, and to give Him the glory.

He was a shy, sick, hard-working, sometimes hard man, who believed that God had laid His hand on him against his will and spent his whole life in obedience. His books have outlasted the city councils, the controversies and the wars of his century. The heart he offered to God has been offered again by countless readers who learned from him to say that they are not their own.

Not unto us, O LORD, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth’s sake. PSALM 115:1
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Go back to the chapter of this book that unsettled you most, and work through its application points again.

2. Begin reading the Institutes for yourself this month, starting with the chapters on the Christian life (3.6–10).

3. Write down one fault you have seen in Calvin that you also find in yourself, and bring it to God.

4. Make the offering of your heart part of your daily prayer for the next month.

5. Tell one other person what you have learned from Calvin, and invite them to read him with you.

A PRAYER
Lord God, the fountain of all good, true wisdom is to know You and to know ourselves in Your light.
Thank You for Your servant John Calvin: for his clear mind, his reverent heart, his long labour for Your church. Forgive us where we have followed him into sin, and keep us where he followed You.
Let us look to You, rest in Christ, and give You our hearts, promptly and sincerely.
To You, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, be all the glory, now and for ever. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to John Calvin
fields.body_html:
Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18

Calvin wrote a great deal: the Institutes, commentaries on most of the Bible, thousands of sermons, treatises, catechisms and letters. All of it is in the public domain in the original French and Latin, and a large part is freely available in older English translations, above all those published by the Calvin Translation Society in Edinburgh in the nineteenth century. The difficulty is not access but choice. What follows is a short map.

Begin here

The Christian life (Institutes 3.6–10). Begin with these five short chapters on self-denial, cross-bearing, meditation on the future life and the right use of this life. They have often been printed on their own, sometimes as The Golden Booklet of the True Christian Life. Nothing Calvin wrote is warmer or more practical.

The sermons in the Ochorus library. Four of Calvin’s sermons are in the Ochorus library, in older English translations: All Scripture Is Given by Inspiration, God Will Have All Men to Be Saved, The Mystery of Godliness and Enduring Persecution for Christ. They show Calvin as his congregation heard him: plain, urgent, sometimes fierce, always pointing to Christ.

The Institutes

Institutes of the Christian Religion. His great work, in its final edition of 1559. It is long, but it is clear and well ordered, and it can be read a chapter at a time. Henry Beveridge’s translation (1845) and John Allen’s (1813) are both in the public domain and freely available. The modern standard edition, translated by Ford Lewis Battles and edited by John T. McNeill (1960), has excellent notes. Read Book 1 on God the Creator and Book 3 on how we receive the grace of Christ first; Book 4 on the church can wait.

The 1536 Institutes. The first edition, much shorter, arranged like a catechism. It is a good introduction to the young Calvin and his defence of the persecuted French believers.

Commentaries and sermons

The Commentaries. Calvin commented on most of the Bible. The Calvin Translation Society edition is freely available. His commentary on the Psalms, whose preface contains the only account he gave of his conversion, is the best place to start; the commentaries on Romans, John and Hebrews are close behind. They are plain, careful and full of devotion.

The Sermons. Calvin preached thousands of sermons, many of which were taken down as he spoke. Sixteenth-century English translations of his sermons on Job, Deuteronomy, Galatians, Ephesians and the pastoral epistles were widely read by the Puritans, and some have been reprinted.

Shorter writings

Reply to Sadoleto (1539). Calvin’s answer to a cardinal who invited Geneva back to Rome. Courteous, clear and one of the best short statements of why the Reformers believed reformation was necessary.

Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper (1541). His teaching on the Supper, written for ordinary readers, and more irenic than his later polemics.

The Genevan Catechism. His teaching of the faith for children, in question and answer, beginning with the chief end of human life.

His Letters. Collected in several volumes in the nineteenth century, they show the pastor at work, especially his letters to prisoners and persecuted churches in France.

About Calvin

Theodore Beza, his friend and successor, wrote a short Life of Calvin soon after his death; it is admiring but invaluable. Among modern lives, T. H. L. Parker’s John Calvin: A Biography (1975) is clear and sympathetic. Bruce Gordon’s Calvin (2009) is a full and balanced modern study, honest about his faults. William J. Bouwsma’s John Calvin: A Sixteenth-Century Portrait (1988) is searching and more critical. François Wendel’s Calvin: The Origins and Development of His Religious Thought remains a fine guide to his theology.

Approach with care

His writings against Servetus and on the punishment of heretics, and his fiercer polemics against his opponents on the Lord’s Supper, are part of the record and should be read with the cautions raised in this book in mind. So should the chapters on predestination and reprobation (Institutes 3.21–24). Roland Bainton’s Hunted Heretic (1953) tells the story of Servetus from the other side, and every admirer of Calvin should read it.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him slowly. Calvin wrote for people who would ponder each sentence. A chapter a day of the Institutes, read with a Bible open, will take you far.

Read him as a pastor. He wrote as a shepherd of troubled souls and persecuted churches, not as an academic. Look for the comfort in his doctrine; he always meant it to be there.

Read him under Scripture. He would insist on it. He wanted nothing more than that his readers would go from his books to the Bible and find God there. Hold fast what agrees with the Word of God, let go what does not, and give thanks for the one who taught so many to say that they are not their own.

For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven. PSALM 119:89

Commentaries and sermons The Commentaries. Calvin commented on most of the Bible. The Calvin Translation Society edition is freely available. His commentary on the Psalms, whose preface contains the only account he gave of his conversion, is the best place to start; the commentaries on Romans, John and Hebrews are close behind. They are plain, careful and full of devotion. The Sermons. Calvin preached thousands of sermons, many of which were taken down as he spoke. Sixteenth-century English translations of his sermons on Job, Deuteronomy, Galatians, Ephesians and the pastoral epistles were widely read by the Puritans, and some have been reprinted. Shorter writings Reply to Sadoleto (1539). Calvin’s answer to a cardinal who invited Geneva back to Rome. Courteous, clear and one of the best short statements of why the Reformers believed reformation was necessary. Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper (1541). His teaching on the Supper, written for ordinary readers, and more irenic than his later polemics. The Genevan Catechism. His teaching of the faith for children, in question and answer, beginning with the chief end of human life. His Letters. Collected in several volumes in the nineteenth century, they show the pastor at work, especially his letters to prisoners and persecuted churches in France. About Calvin Theodore Beza, his friend and successor, wrote a short Life of Calvin soon after his death; it is admiring but invaluable. Among modern lives, T. H. L. Parker’s John Calvin: A Biography (1975) is clear and sympathetic. Bruce Gordon’s Calvin (2009) is a full and balanced modern study, honest about his faults. William J. Bouwsma’s John Calvin: A Sixteenth-Century Portrait (1988) is searching and more critical. François Wendel’s Calvin: The Origins and Development of His Religious Thought remains a fine guide to his theology. Approach with care His writings against Servetus and on the punishment of heretics, and his fiercer polemics against his opponents on the Lord’s Supper, are part of the record and should be read with the cautions raised in this book in mind. So should the chapters on predestination and reprobation (Institutes 3.21–24). Roland Bainton’s Hunted Heretic (1953) tells the story of Servetus from the other side, and every admirer of Calvin should read it. Three counsels for reading him Read him slowly. Calvin wrote for people who would ponder each sentence. A chapter a day of the Institutes, read with a Bible open, will take you far. Read him as a pastor. He wrote as a shepherd of troubled souls and persecuted churches, not as an academic. Look for the comfort in his doctrine; he always meant it to be there. Read him under Scripture. He would insist on it. He wanted nothing more than that his readers would go from his books to the Bible and find God there. Hold fast what agrees with the Word of God, let go what does not, and give thanks for the one who taught so many to say that they are not their own. For ever, O LORD, thy word is settled in heaven.
